articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1707: UN commission finds Russia’s strikes on Ukraine’s power grid are crimes against humanity
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Ukraine intercepts nearly 60% of Russia’s Geran-4 jet drones, General Staff says, as Kyiv races to counter evolving threat. Ukraine’s interception rate reaches 80% during some attacks, as F-16s, Mirage jets, mobile fire groups, and interceptor drones help counter Russia’s jet-powered attacks.
He drove a taxi in Jakarta and once worked in the US. Russia trained him as a machine gunner for a week and a half, then sent him into his first and last battle. Ukraine’s military intelligence says Russian recruiters reached the Indonesian through his job search and moved him from a contract signing near Moscow to the front in a matter of weeks.
Russia tries to drag a village north of Kupiansk into no-man’s-land after its losses in Ukraine’s underground operation. Ukraine’s military describes Russian troops trying to keep a path open toward the city through Radkivka, a village on its northern edge, while fighting for neighboring Holubivka goes on.
Ukraine says it hit drone hangars at Crimea’s Hvardiiske. Now an OSINT channel spots 20+ bermed shelters there. Dnipro Osint says the base fires Shahed-type drones from vehicles on its runway, and the airfield kept turning up on Ukraine’s launch lists in October.
Two weeks after a Russian supply base burned in Luhansk’s Khrustalnyi, Ukrainian drones came back for an ammo depot. The city in occupied eastern Ukraine has served Russia’s army as a rear logistics hub since early in the full-scale war.
Ukraine plans to rebuild its air force on NATO’s model by 2035. Its Air Force already knows which fighter it wants next, and why. Ukraine’s F-16s face thousands of Russian targets a month, many of them worn jets bought secondhand.
For the third time this year, Ukrainian drones hit Russia’s rocket-fuel rubber plant in Samara Oblast. This time they reach the raw-material shop feeding it. OSINT channels recorded fires at the same butyl-rubber shops in April and September.
Intelligence and technology
Germany’s Helsing promises jet-drone-hunting missiles at under $100,000 a shot—its CEO doesn’t expect them on the market before 2027. One contract is signed. Ukraine’s own jet-drone interceptors, meanwhile, aren’t due in needed numbers before late November.
Ukraine says it has finished its part of FREYJA, Europe’s joint anti-ballistic project. Partners’ work is still underway. Zelenskyy told ABC News on 23 October that Ukraine got only 24 US Patriot interceptors from the US in three months.
Postal service Nova Post says it has already shot down Russian Shahed drones, as Ukrainian businesses take air defense into their own hands. The company says its air defense project is operational as Russia increasingly targets Ukrainian infrastructure, while other businesses weigh the costs and benefits of protecting their facilities themselves.
Ukrainian intelligence says Russia’s missile makers use gear from seven countries—and the Chinese machines run on European, Japanese, and Taiwanese parts. Ukrainian intelligence listed 30 foreign-made items at Russian arms plants on 26 October, 17 of them made outside China.
A 4-watt video link passed Ukraine’s state tests, its maker says, and could stretch STING interceptors’ radius from 20 km to 30 km. The 30 km figure is Wild Hornets’ own estimate, first given in August, and assumes good line of sight. Testers checked three drone types.
Captured Russians say there is one place on Kupiansk front they will not go: “Orion” safety corridor. Ukrainian robot unit says it built that corridor, and runs supply and evacuation through it with almost no losses.
Ukrainian intelligence: Russia can probably add 10–15 Su-34 bombers a year, but no new Tu-95s or Tu-22M3s. Ukraine’s military intelligence also listed Russian jets destroyed or critically damaged in 2026, including two Tu-95MS bombers hit at Engels.
International
Finland and Norway leaders make rare direct call to Putin, breaking with the West’s diplomatic isolation of the Russian leader to influence Ukraine peace talks. The Nordic leaders called for de-escalation ahead of November peace talks, with Zelenskyy saying they pressed Putin over attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. The Kremlin reiterated that any settlement must account for Russia’s demands.
Ukraine’s last two EU negotiation blocks stay shut as Hungary’s new government keeps Orbán’s veto. Budapest unblocked half of the remaining negotiations after Ukraine changed its minority-language rules, then said no to the rest.
The Trump administration is backing Orbán, who blocked a €90 billion EU loan to Ukraine, for UN secretary-general and is counting on support from Moscow and Beijing, WSJ says. Orbán indicated that he was willing to consider the nomination but did not want to enter the race without being confident he could win, according to the WSJ’s editorial board.
Ukraine’s Zelenskyy welcomes Student List’s win in Serbia and says Kyiv is “ready to keep increasing cooperation”. The party itself plan to end the trade that brought Ukraine €800 million in ammunition.
17 public broadcasters mapped Russia’s hybrid war on Europe. Germany: four dots. One point on the map may stand for several incidents of the same type nearby or in quick succession.
Humanitarian and social impact
Russia replaces Ukrainians with Russian settlers in occupied Kherson Oblast; only 10–20% of pre-war population remains, Ukraine says. Russia is forcing Ukrainians from their homes while offering Russian teachers and medical workers financial incentives to settle in occupied Kherson Oblast, Ukraine’s military intelligence says.
Oleshky ceasefire expands beyond occupied town as truce holds without reported violations. The expanded ceasefire zone aims to secure humanitarian convoys to Russian-occupied Oleshky, where residents face shortages of food and medicine.
Russia strikes publishing house warehouse in Kharkiv on Ukrainian Language Day, adding to a campaign against Ukrainian literature and culture. The publisher is assessing losses after the attack disrupted its planned 5 November releases, as repeated Russian strikes destroy books and damage Ukraine’s publishing industry.
Guns fall silent around Russian-occupied Oleshky so its starving residents can get aid, but Russia’s guarantees remain secret. Ukraine’s ombudsman says both sides are keeping to the deal, while the US first lady’s adviser says Newsmax will send reporters to watch whether residents can leave freely.
Russian ballistic missiles hit a Kyiv university campus, then return before dawn for the Southern Bridge again. Two waves hit the capital hours apart, reaching students in their dormitory in the evening and the bridge carrying its green metro line before sunrise.
Sixteen Ukrainian doctors who work near fighting went through three Western trauma programs in one week. American surgeons led drills. On the front line, drones and shrapnel often tear through several parts of a soldier’s body at once.
Political and legal developments
Russian court jails IT company director for 13 years over crypto donations after Binance shared his data, rights group says. The man had lived in Bulgaria for about 10 years before flying to Moscow on business last year, where he was detained at the airport for allegedly using obscene language.
UN commission finds Russia’s grid strikes are crimes against humanity, citing last winter at minus 21°C. Now they’re intensifying. The commission concluded the strikes followed a state policy to deprive civilians of power and cause suffering, and noted that Russian authorities had openly announced further attacks and referred to a plan to carry them out.

articles.title: Netanyahu panics over Arab turnout; Likud seeks vote extension
articles.body:
Israel exit polls show deadlock as Arab parties make history
Millions of Israelis are headed to the polls on Tuesday amid a record-turnout in the country's first general elections since the start of the genocidal Gaza war
This live blog has now ended. Make sure to follow us for the latest news on Facebook, X, and Instagram.
The first exit polls from Israel's pivotal general election on Tuesday showed strong gains for the country's Arab-majority parties, whose voter base turned out in high numbers. Exit polls from the main Israeli television channels showed the two Arab lists winning 17 or 18 seats in the 120-member parliament between them, up from 10 in the last election in 2022.
Israel has so far recorded the highest voter turnout since 1973 as millions of people head to the polls to elect 120 members of the Knesset. Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank are not allowed to vote, despite the Israeli government determining the direction of their future.
Israeli voters on Tuesday gave a narrow edge to opposition parties over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, initial projections showed, after decades-high turnout in the country's first election since the outbreak of the genocidal war.
The southern West Bank city of Hebron remains besieged for the fifth consecutive day following a deadly shootout on Friday, which prompted a large military operation that has displaced nearly 4,000 Palestinians.
Meanwhile, the war in Yemen rages, with the Saudi-led coalition intercepting Houthi ballistic missiles and Houthi-affiliated media reported that Yemeni government forces launched air strikes in Taiz province
Opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot said early Wednesday said Israel had chosen change after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and that he would seek to form a new government.
In remarks to supporters, Eisenkot also issued a veiled warning to Netanyahu who has stepped up warnings in the final days of the campaign that he will attack Iran -- an emergency that could potentially delay efforts to form a coalition.
"Netanyahu, don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.
Exit polls showed the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot with a tiny edge over Netanyahu's right-wing bloc in Tuesday's election but with neither side securing a majority.
"The people have spoken against the continuation of Netanyahu's rule," Eisenkot said.
"In an election with such a high turnout, it would be a mistake to go to another round of elections."
Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted Houthi missile
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said early on Wednesday that it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by Yemen's Houthis towards the western Saudi city of Taif, as cross-border hostilities between the kingdom and the Iran-aligned group have intensified.
Saudi Civil Defense issued early warning alerts for a potential hostile threat in Jeddah and Yanbu governorates, before saying minutes later that the danger had passed in both areas.
Pezeshkian tells Putin region can solve problems without US
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin on Tuesday that the Middle East can solve its problems without the involvement of the United States.
"I believe we are capable of resolving our problems in the region without relying on the United States," Pezeshkian said at a meeting with Putin on the sidelines of a summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum in Moscow.
"Our trade is expanding and growing day by day. US actions in the region make it easier for us to move towards greater multilateralism and strengthen our cooperation with you and other countries subject to unilateral US sanctions," he told Putin.
Putin said he discussed the war with Pezeshkian, expressing hope that the situation would improve.
Israel FM says opposition celebrations 'premature'
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said opposition celebrations were "premature" after initial exit polls in Tuesday's election showed it with a slight edge over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing bloc led by Likud.
"The celebrations on the left are premature. The smugness of the biased commentators -- ridiculous. One thing seems quite clear: (Netanyahu's) Likud is the largest party in Israel," he said on X, posting a video showing Likud's first election win in 1977.
UN nuclear watchdog chief urges Iran to grant access
IAEA chief Rafael Grossi urged Iran during a UN Security Council meeting on Tuesday to grant immediate access to his agency so it can verify the Islamic republic's nuclear materials.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since Israel, joined by the United States, launched a 12-day conflict in June 2025 that included strikes on nuclear sites.
Nuclear facilities have also been hit in the latest war, which erupted on February 28, and the IAEA has repeatedly called for access.
"I invite Iran to work with the IAEA without any further delay to clarify outstanding safeguards questions and to give the IAEA the information and access the agency requires, so that it can verify all relevant facilities and material, as is Iran's legal obligation," Grossi said.
The Security Council meeting followed a resolution passed by the IAEA board last month that referred Iran to the top UN body over its nuclear "non-compliance."
Eisenkot: Election results show 'lack of confidence'
Gadi Eisenkot, the main election challenger to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, said on Tuesday that the initial exit polls from the country's pivotal vote showed a "complete lack of confidence" in the veteran premier.
"The initial exit poll results indicate a complete lack of confidence in Netanyahu and the October 7 government," Eisenkot said. Israel's current opposition chief Yair Lapid said Netanyahu's bloc had suffered a "crushing defeat", while left-wing leader Yair Golan said the public had "fired the Netanyahu government".
Strong gains for Arab-majority parties in Israel vote: polls
The first exit polls from Israel's pivotal general election on Tuesday showed strong gains for the country's Arab-majority parties, whose voter base turned out in high numbers.
Exit polls from the main Israeli television channels showed the two Arab lists winning 17 or 18 seats in the 120-member parliament between them, up from 10 in the last election in 2022.
First Israeli election exit polls show narrow edge
The first exit polls from Israel's elections showed the opposition bloc with a slight edge over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's camp as voting ended Tuesday, but still shy of an outright majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
The country's main pollsters, Channels 11, 12, and 13, projected the opposition bloc to win between 52 and 54 seats, and Netanyahu's bloc to win around 50, although his Likud would be the largest single party in parliament, with 24 or 25 seats.
Yemen's Houthis said they fired missiles at Saudi Arabia's biggest oil refinery and its defence ministry on Tuesday as the Iran-backed group kept up its weeks-long wave of attacks.
Saudi Arabia, the world's top exporter of crude, has suffered constant Houthi strikes against oil and civilian sites this month, including Riyadh's international airport.
The Houthis said they attacked the defence ministry in Riyadh and the Ras Tanura refinery on the east coast among a series of attacks across the sprawling desert kingdom on Tuesday.
"Our armed forces targeted the Ministry of Defence in the enemy Saudi capital, Riyadh, with a ballistic missile and the hit was direct," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said.
The Houthis were also "able to target the Ras Tanura refinery in the Eastern Province with a ballistic missile", he said in a separate post.
UN nuclear watchdog chief urges Iran to grant access
IAEA chief Rafael Grossi urged Iran during a UN Security Council meeting on Tuesday to grant immediate access to his agency so it can verify the Islamic Republic's nuclear materials.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since Israel, joined by the United States, launched a 12-day war in June 2025 that included strikes on nuclear sites.
Nuclear facilities have also been hit in the latest war, which erupted on 28 February, and the IAEA has repeatedly called for access.
"I invite Iran to work with the IAEA without any further delay to clarify outstanding safeguards questions and to give the IAEA the information and access the agency requires, so that it can verify all relevant facilities and material, as is Iran's legal obligation," Grossi said.
The Security Council meeting followed a resolution the IAEA board passed last month that referred Iran to the UN's top body over its nuclear "non-compliance."
Israel election commission rejects Netanyahu extension bid
Israel's Central Elections Committee on Tuesday rejected a request by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party to extend voting beyond 10 PM (2000 GMT).
"High nationwide turnout across all sectors of society reflects strong public engagement in the democratic process, and no need to extend voting hours was identified," a commission statement said.
Voter turnout in the Israeli elections has reached 66.7% as of 6pm, according to the Central Elections Committee, a record high as of this time in the day.
Pezeshkian tells Putin region can solve problems without US
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin on Tuesday that the Middle East can solve its problems without the involvement of the United States.
"I believe we are capable of resolving our problems in the region without relying on the United States," Pezeshkian said at a meeting with Putin on the sidelines of a summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum in Moscow.
Eisenkot's Yashar opposes bid to extend Israel voting hours
The party of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main election challenger said it "firmly opposes" a call from the premier's party to extend voting hours on Tuesday, calling it a pretext for a future challenge to the poll's legitimacy.
"No exceptional incident has occurred that would justify granting this request, which is intended to lay the groundwork for allegations challenging the integrity of the election, continuing the lies Netanyahu has been spreading since this morning," ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party said.
Meanwhile, Shas and Jewish Power have joined Likud's request for an extension.
Mansour Abbas accuses Netanyahu of 'lying, inciting'
The leader of a key Israeli Arab party accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of incitement through his allegations of fraud on behalf of the minority group in Tuesday's elections.
"Benjamin Netanyahu is lying and inciting against the United Arab List, using it as a scare tactic to mobilise right-wing voters and drive them to the polls," the list's leader Mansour Abbas said in a video message.
Canada and the UAE to sign trade deal on Tuesday: report
Canada and the United Arab Emirates will sign a comprehensive trade deal on Tuesday to lower barriers between the two economies and boost investment, a source familiar with the plan said, as Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks to expand trade and investment ties at a time of tension with the United States.
Prime Minister Mark Carney will participate in a signing ceremony with the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi at 1 p.m. ET (1700 GMT), Carney's schedule says.
The agreement, formally called the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, will be signed by International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu and his Emirati counterpart, Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi, the source said.
As President Donald Trump's tariffs rippled through Canada's economy and subsequent attempts for a deal with Washington have broken down, Carney vowed to double Ottawa's non-US trade over the next decade. He has aggressively pursued trade pacts across the world and his team and chased deals with countries from the Asia Pacific to Europe and Middle East.
The signing is the last step before Canada’s Parliament can ratify the agreement, that source said.
Fresh clashes in Yemen kill 97 combatants: military sources
Nearly 100 fighters have been killed in renewed clashes between Yemen's Houthis and government forces in southwestern Yemen, military sources from both sides told AFP on Tuesday.
At least 63 Houthi fighters and 34 pro-government combatants have died, mostly near the Bab al-Mandab strait, the Red Sea's strategic southern chokepoint, they said.
The clashes, which began with airstrikes late on Monday, are the fiercest since the Iran-allied Houthis seized swathes of territory from the Saudi-backed government in a lightning offensive last month.
The Houthis fought off "an attempted advance by Saudi enemy forces... from the southern direction of Bab al-Mandab", military spokesman Yahya Saree posted on X, describing "a large number of dead and wounded".
The Houthi military sources said Saudi Arabia carried out dozens of airstrikes, hitting Mayyun Island in the strait as well as Dhubab and Mocha further up the Red Sea coast.
Government military sources said intense fighting was under way in the Bab al-Mandab area, claiming they had made progress on the ground.
Judge orders Spanish gov declassify more material on Ceuta
A Spanish judge investigating July's mass migrant crossing into Ceuta from Morocco told the government on Tuesday to declassify further intelligence documents and reports related to the deadly border rush, a court ruling showed.
High Court Judge Maria Tardon is probing what Spanish authorities knew in advance about the crossing, how that intelligence was handled and whether officials failed to act on warnings. She gave the cabinet 15 days to comply.
Netanyahu's party asks to extend Israeli election hours
Palestinian citizens of Israel turned out in significant numbers on Tuesday, seeking to punish Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right government in the country's parliamentary elections.
Arab voters account for around 18% of the electorate, with pre-election projections suggesting participation could rise substantially from the previous vote.
Analysts told The New Arab that stronger Arab turnout could prevent some far-right parties from entering parliament and complicate Netanyahu's efforts to form another coalition. However, they warned that even a change of government would be unlikely to bring an immediate shift in Israel's policies towards Palestinians.
Iran needs to show good intentions for mediation efforts to succeed, mediator Qatar said on Tuesday, after a delegation from the Gulf Arab country visited Tehran earlier this week in an effort to de-escalate regional tensions in coordination with the United States.
A spokesperson for the Qatari Foreign Ministry told a press briefing that Iran should stop threats against Arab Gulf states and open the Strait of Hormuz to show good intentions.
Qatar, along with Pakistan, has been mediating between Washington and Tehran in an effort to end the US-Israeli war on Iran that has disrupted global shipping and oil supplies, and spilled over across other parts of the Middle East.
Top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan also met Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday in an effort to de-escalate the conflict, as Yemen's Houthis launched new attacks on Saudi Arabia and Egypt approved defence support for the Gulf kingdom.
Tensions between Washington and Tehran have sharpened recently, with President Donald Trump saying on Friday the US may strike Iran again. Iranian security officials told Reuters Tehran had drawn up detailed plans to attack Gulf undersea cables if the US and Israel attack again.
Iraqi court jails French nationals for belonging to IS
An Iraqi court on Tuesday sentenced seven French nationals to prison for belonging to the Islamic State group, after they were transferred along with dozens of others from Syria last year.
Six of the defendants were handed life sentences, which under Iraqi law is equivalent to 20 years in prison.
They were found guilty of belonging to IS and "of having contributed, together with members of the group, to spreading terror", according to an AFP journalist at the court.
The judge told the defendants the court had "commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment, given that you are young, in order to offer you a chance... to get your life back on track".
The court sentenced a seventh French national to 15 years in prison. The now 24-year-old had been taken to Syria by his mother, who joined IS more than a decade ago.
All seven were part of a group of 47 French citizens transferred from Syria last year.
The larger group includes Adrien Guihal, who claimed responsibility for the 2016 Nice attack for IS.
Yemen's Houthis say targeted Saudi defence ministry in Riyad
Yemen's Houthis on Tuesday said they targeted the Saudi defence ministry in the capital Riyadh, where authorities earlier said they had intercepted missiles launched by the group.
"Our armed forces targeted the Ministry of Defence in the enemy Saudi capital, Riyadh, with a ballistic missile and the hit was direct," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said.

articles.title: Putin and Pezeshkian Honor Khamenei, Killed in US-Israeli Strikes, and Challenge US Influence
articles.body:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday, Oct. 27, that the Middle East could resolve its conflicts without the US, as Tehran and Moscow pledged to deepen an increasingly consequential partnership spanning military cooperation, energy and regional security.
Speaking on the sidelines of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow, Pezeshkian thanked Putin for Russia’s political and economic support and called for closer cooperation among countries facing US sanctions.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I believe we are capable of resolving our problems in the region without relying on the US,” Pezeshkian said.
He argued that Washington’s actions were encouraging Iran and Russia to work more closely together and strengthen a multipolar international order.
“Our trade is expanding and growing day by day. US actions in the region make it easier for us to move towards greater multilateralism and strengthen our cooperation with you and other countries subject to unilateral US sanctions,” he said.
The statements highlighted the deepening relationship between two governments whose military cooperation has already had direct consequences for Ukraine.
Iran has supplied Russia with drones and ballistic missile technology used to support its invasion of Ukraine, according to US and European authorities. Moscow, meanwhile, has reportedly provided Iran with military equipment, drone technology and intelligence assistance amid its confrontation with Washington and Israel.
Zelensky Urges US to End Month-Long Patriot Missile Delay as Russian Strikes Kill Civilians
The cooperation has raised concerns that technology and battlefield experience gained in Russia’s war against Ukraine could also strengthen Iranian military capabilities in the Middle East.
From Iranian drones in Ukraine to Russian military assistance for Tehran
The Russia-Iran relationship has evolved beyond diplomatic coordination and economic cooperation into an increasingly important military partnership.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Iranian-designed Shahed drones have become a major component of Moscow’s long-range strike campaign.
Russia subsequently established domestic production and modified the drones, improving their capabilities for use against Ukrainian targets.
US and European officials have reported that Russia may be transferring upgraded Shahed drones back to Iran, incorporating improvements developed during the war in Ukraine.
Putin and Pezeshkian Pay Tribute to Ayatollah Khamenei, Killed in US-Israeli Strikes
During Tuesday’s talks, Pezeshkian expressed confidence that Moscow and Tehran could deepen cooperation across several sectors, explicitly including security and military affairs.
He thanked Putin for supporting Iran politically and economically, arguing that US pressure had created greater incentives for countries under sanctions to cooperate.
“After the Americans began taking such aggressive steps in the region, it became clear to everyone that we must work toward creating a multipolar world,” Pezeshkian said.
His remarks came amid the continuing confrontation involving Iran, the US and Israel, which escalated with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov visited Tehran last week. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi subsequently said the two countries had never worked so closely.
Both leaders paid tribute to Iran’s late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in US-Israeli strikes on Feb. 28.
Addressing the Gas Exporting Countries Forum, Pezeshkian praised Khamenei’s foresight, initiative and support for the organization, describing his contribution to its development as substantial.
Putin echoed the tribute, crediting Khamenei with playing an active role in establishing the forum.
“You rightly recalled the role of the former spiritual leader of the Iranian people, Ayatollah Khamenei, who was indeed one of the active participants in establishing our forum,” Putin said.
“We rightly remember him with gratitude.”
Iran Approves Russian State TV Bureau in Tehran as Ties Deepen
Putin used the meeting to emphasize the economic foundations of the partnership.
He said bilateral trade increased by 10.4% during the first eight months of 2026 and reaffirmed Moscow’s commitment to ongoing joint projects.
“We are fulfilling all our obligations under all our projects,” Putin said.
The Russian president highlighted continued construction at Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant, where Russia is a major technology and construction partner.
He also noted that nearly 10,000 Iranian students were enrolled at Russian universities.
Pezeshkian announced that Iran had cleared the way for Russia’s state television broadcaster VGTRK to establish a bureau in Tehran, following discussions during Lavrov’s recent visit.
The expansion of Russian state media operations would add another dimension to an increasingly broad relationship involving government institutions, energy companies and security establishments.
Putin and Pezeshkian challenge Western energy sanctions
At the gas exporters’ summit, both presidents criticized Western sanctions and efforts to restrict their countries’ participation in international energy markets.
Pezeshkian accused the US and Israel of undermining global energy security through military attacks on Iranian infrastructure and restrictions affecting the country’s energy exports.
He urged major gas-producing countries to oppose what he described as destabilizing unilateral measures.
Putin echoed those criticisms, arguing that Europe’s efforts to reduce dependence on Russian gas were harming European industries and households.
“Any attempts to exclude Russia from the global gas market or restrain the development of our industry carry serious consequences,” he said.
The Russian president accused European governments of imposing excessive costs on their own economies by rejecting Russian energy supplies.
The EU has pursued restrictions on Russian energy imports as part of broader efforts to reduce the revenue available to Moscow for financing its war against Ukraine.
Putin explores US energy cooperation despite Tehran’s anti-US message
Despite Pezeshkian’s call to reduce US influence in the Middle East, Putin signaled that Moscow remained open to cooperation with American companies in the energy sector.
Speaking at the forum, Putin said Russia was considering joint projects with US partners in the Arctic.
“Until recently, European partners worked alongside us in our fields, and Chinese partners are still working there. Now, we’re exploring the possibility of joint work with American partners,” Putin said.
He did not identify prospective American companies or specific agreements.

articles.title: France and 10 European countries plan to deploy nuclear-capable French jets to deter Russia, WSJ reports
articles.body:
France and 10 European countries plan to deploy nuclear-capable French jets to deter Russia, WSJ reports
France is working with 10 other European countries to establish a new nuclear deterrence framework aimed at Russia, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The initiative, which President Emmanuel Macron called “forward deterrence,” was unveiled in March 2026. It calls for deploying nuclear-capable French Rafale fighter jets to other European countries. Participants also intend to create a joint system for early warning and intelligence sharing.
The United Kingdom, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Poland, Greece, Finland, Norway, Sweden, and Denmark have joined France in the initiative. The three Baltic states, which are most vulnerable to Russian aggression, are not part of the project, while Italy declined to participate. Finland said it would like to take part but does not plan to host nuclear weapons on its territory in peacetime.
French officials believe the new deterrent could be more credible because the security of France’s European neighbors matters far more to Paris than to Washington.
European officials also emphasize that the new system should supplement, rather than replace, the American “nuclear umbrella” over the continent and create further strategic uncertainty for Russia.
Experts say the French ASMP-A cruise missiles carried by Rafale fighters are more effective in modern warfare than American B-61 nuclear bombs. The American bombs were developed in the 1960s, and advances in Russian air defenses limit their use.
Macron also said France plans to resume producing nuclear weapons for the first time in decades. The country currently has about 290 nuclear warheads but will no longer disclose information about its arsenal.
In practice, however, France will retain full control over its nuclear forces. “The French will let us participate in their nuclear deterrence as much as the Americans,” said a minister from one of the countries involved in the project.
France is holding bilateral talks with its partners and has set up 10 separate groups for those discussions. Defense officials across Europe have had to hold frequent calls to keep one another informed about the negotiations, military officials said.

articles.title: Tokyo can create means of delivering nuclear weapons, China says
articles.body:
BEIJING, October 28. /TASS/. Japan has the industrial and technical potential to develop delivery systems for nuclear weapons, Secretary General of the China Arms Control and Disarmament Association (CACDA) Dai Huaicheng told TASS.
According to him, Japan has been actively expanding its military capabilities in recent years by acquiring advanced US weapons. Besides, it has its own technologies that can be used for military purposes, Dai Huaicheng said.
"Japan has long held a leading position in the world in the field of large launch vehicles, has mastered the key technologies necessary for the development of medium-and long-range ballistic missiles, such as guidance and reentry systems, and also has the technical base for the development of ships with a nuclear power plant," he said.
"This means that if it makes the relevant political decision, Japan will face no insurmountable industrial and technical obstacles either in the field of nuclear warheads or in their delivery systems.
"Japan is the only non-nuclear-weapon state party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons that possesses nuclear fuel reprocessing technologies, is capable of extracting weapons-grade plutonium and has operating fuel reprocessing facilities, as well as the only country outside the nuclear club that has a full-fledged nuclear fuel cycle. In addition, Japan has a powerful industrial base and economic potential, which theoretically enable it to produce and obtain nuclear materials using existing reactors and reprocessing technologies to manufacture nuclear explosive devices."
According to Dai Huaicheng, Japan has been building up its military potential in recent years with support from the US military industry.
"As for the means of delivery, the F-35A, F-15 and F-2 fighters in service with the Japan Air Self-Defense Forces are potentially capable of carrying nuclear bombs. Japan has also decided to purchase several hundred Tomahawk cruise missiles, modify the launchers on ships equipped with the Aegis combat information management system, and deploy US Typhon medium-range ground-based missiles," he said.

articles.title: Zelensky Warns of Russia’s ‘Economic Marriage’ With US as Ukraine Feels ‘Home Alone’ Without Patriots
articles.body:
Russia could offer the US an “economic marriage” built on energy and other economic deals, but it would likely come at a cost in the long run, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
“I believe the ‘diesel deal’ opens the door for the Russians to take further similar steps,” Zelensky told journalists, as quoted by Ukrainian media.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He suggested that future agreements could involve fertilizers, gas, frozen assets, and the lifting of sanctions on specific individuals and entities.
He revealed that sanctions had already been lifted on Russian oligarchs close to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“Russia understands that – unlike other nations – it possesses such natural resources, capabilities, reserves, and a centralized, vertical control over all of this, that it could genuinely propose a sort of ‘economic marriage’ to America – as unpleasant as that may sound,” Zelensky said.
However, he said that such an arrangement might not benefit Washington in the long run, even if it appeared advantageous initially.
“Every deal involving Russia contains some unpleasant element that isn’t immediately apparent – even if, in the short term, it might seem like there are benefits to be gained,” he said.
Russia’s security demands and NATO
Zelensky warned that NATO should not agree to Russia’s demands for security guarantees while Moscow continues its war against Ukraine.
Putin Lectured Nordic Leaders on History, Zelensky Reveals Kyiv’s Role
“If you want security guarantees for Ukraine, then we want them for Russia,” the Russian side has argued, according to Zelensky.
He said Moscow’s demands go far beyond assurances that Ukraine would not attack Russian territory, instead seeking a broader agreement with NATO or the US.
Zelensky added that Russia had raised similar demands before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Moscow could again seek NATO’s withdrawal from certain territories or the removal of Alliance infrastructure, he said.
Such decisions, he stressed, rest with NATO member states – not Russia or Ukraine. Zelensky also warned that any rollback in security would signal weakness for the Alliance.
“One cannot discuss any global security guarantees for Russia while it remains unclear how – and on what basis – their war against Ukraine will end, and before we know what security guarantees Ukraine itself will have,” he said.
Zelensky added that the issue of the war must be resolved before Russia’s demands regarding the European and global security architecture can be addressed.
He also acknowledged that Washington had sent signals about a possible reduction in the number of US troops stationed in Europe.
Middle East war affects Ukraine’s air defense
Zelensky said the war in the Middle East had negatively affected military and financial support for Ukraine, including supplies of air defense missiles. He pointed to the situation around the Strait of Hormuz as one factor contributing to global energy pressures.
According to Zelensky, Ukraine received just 12 US missiles per month for its Patriot air defense systems throughout 2026.
He said the amount was far below Ukraine’s needs, as Russia launches approximately 150 ballistic missiles against the country each month.
Even if Ukraine received 150 US interceptor missiles a year, Zelensky said, it would still face a significant gap between available supplies and the demands of defending against Russian attacks.
Ukraine is working with partners to secure additional anti-ballistic missiles, but transfers of US-made interceptors require approval from US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, he added.
Zelensky said several issues had converged in Ukraine’s relations with Washington, including Starlink and Starshield, intelligence sharing, interceptor missile supplies, and agreements concerning Russian diesel.
“We understand where things are heading. It’s like the next installment of Home Alone. It is a challenge – a tough challenge,” he said.
The president also said Ukraine had provided assistance to Middle Eastern partners at their request, including support related to bases hosting American personnel in Saudi Arabia and the UAE. He added that ending the regional crisis was important for Ukraine, too.
Ukraine and US resume intelligence sharing
Separately, Zelensky confirmed that Ukraine and the US had resumed intelligence sharing, thanking US President Donald Trump, military officials, and others who helped make the decision possible.
“We are grateful to our American partners – to everyone who made this happen: President Donald Trump, the military, and everyone else who helped,” Zelensky said.

articles.title: US urges Gulf allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes after midterms, report says
articles.body:
The United States has urged several Arab Gulf countries to prepare for a short but intense military campaign against Iran following next week's U.S. midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday, citing people briefed on discussions between Washington and regional governments.
According to the report, the messages, delivered through diplomatic and military channels, are among a growing number of indications that the United States and Israel are preparing for another round of large-scale military operations against Iran.
U.S. President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on whether to launch an attack but is leaning toward a broad military operation after the midterms, the newspaper reported. Potential targets include Iranian critical infrastructure and nuclear facilities.
The alternative remains a negotiated agreement with Tehran. Regional mediators continue diplomatic efforts to avert another confrontation, but those talks have yet to produce a breakthrough.
The reported preparations include significant changes to the U.S. military posture in the Middle East.
Officials familiar with the matter told the Journal that the U.S. military is moving a Patriot air defense system from Texas to the region to strengthen its defenses against potential Iranian missile attacks.
American forces have also been relocated from bases considered vulnerable to attack as part of preparations for a possible escalation.
According to several officials cited in the report, U.S. troops stationed in the region have replenished their ammunition supplies, while American bombers and fighter jets are being readied for potential strikes.
An additional aircraft carrier strike group and a Marine Corps expeditionary force are expected to join the U.S. military buildup next month, the newspaper reported.
They would augment an armada of roughly 20 warships already operating in the Middle East, although some of the incoming vessels could replace ships currently deployed in the region rather than increase the overall number.
Netanyahu: 'This is not over'
The Journal's report emerged around the same time that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed supporters early Wednesday following Israel's parliamentary election.
Netanyahu's Likud party remained the largest in the Knesset, according to exit polls, although his right-wing political bloc appeared to have lost significant ground, leaving his ability to form a governing coalition uncertain.
Netanyahu opened his election-night address by focusing on Iran, declaring that Israel's confrontation with the Islamic Republic was far from over.
"We have brought the Iranian regime to the brink of collapse," Netanyahu said. "And yet I tell you, this is still not over. Because as long as this fanatical regime exists, a regime that has defined its very purpose as destroying our existence, it will try again to destroy us."
"We have the power, together with our wonderful friend President Trump, to remove this threat once and for all," he added.
Netanyahu's remarks came shortly after his main rival Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar party, called on him to resign, describing him as "a caretaker prime minister without a mandate or public trust."
Eisenkot made the comments Tuesday night, before dramatic overnight revisions to the election exit polls altered the projected balance between the political blocs.
His warning reflected concerns among opposition figures that Netanyahu could seek to escalate security tensions to complicate efforts to replace him or pressure rival parties into joining an emergency government.
Addressing senior defense and security officials, Eisenkot urged them to resist any attempt to involve the security establishment in political maneuvering.
"Stand firm against any attempt to challenge you," he said.
He then directed a warning at Netanyahu: "Do not dare use Israel's security for your political purposes."

articles.title: Italy’s Ukraine aid package stalls ahead of U.S. midterms, report says
articles.body:
- Italy’s 13th military aid package for Ukraine, expected to include Aster 30 missiles, remains frozen ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, La Repubblica reported.
- Rome had promised Macron and Zelenskyy approval by the end of October, but the Copasir committee has not yet been called to review it.
Italy’s 13th military aid package for Ukraine, which is expected to include Aster 30 air defense missiles, is ready but frozen, and Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government appears to be waiting for the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3 before moving it forward, La Repubblica reported Tuesday.
If the delay continues, Rome would miss a deadline it set with French President Emmanuel Macron and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. According to the newspaper, Meloni’s government had promised both leaders the package would be approved by the end of October. With four days left in the month, the parliamentary committee that must be briefed on the package had not been called to meet, and the paper reported no sign that a meeting was imminent.
That committee, known as Copasir, oversees Italy’s intelligence services. Italian aid to Ukraine has been classified since 2022, and the government presents each package to Copasir before it moves forward. The previous 12 packages were authorized through interministerial decrees.
La Repubblica reported that the package has been pushed back several times: first from July, then from September, then until after a congress of the League, a party in Meloni’s governing coalition, and now until after the American vote. The government’s public statements have stayed general, the paper said, and officials in Rome are handling the issue with a mix of caution and embarrassment.
The most pressing item for Kyiv is the Aster 30, an interceptor missile fired by the Franco-Italian SAMP/T air defense system. Ukraine uses it to protect Kyiv and other cities from Russian attacks. Its targets include aircraft, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles. La Repubblica wrote that only Italy, together with France, can supply the missile.
The October deadline traces back to July. After meeting Macron, Zelenskyy said Italy and France would speed up deliveries of Aster 30 missiles so they would arrive by October 2026.
In August, La Repubblica reported that the 13th package would center on air and missile defense. The paper said it would include four SAMP/T NG batteries, the newest version of the system, along with Aster 30 interceptors and seven long-range radars. It put the package’s value at nearly 3 billion euros ($3.5 billion), funded through European Union loans. The Italian government has not confirmed what the package contains.
Defense Minister Guido Crosetto pushed back on those reports at the time. He said they gave the impression the package had already been approved, and that no new aid package for Ukraine had been formally adopted in 2026.
A Copasir briefing planned for Aug. 5 was also postponed, Italian media reported at the time. The reports cited concern in the government about public support and opposition to further arms deliveries from parts of the political right.
La Repubblica reported that Italy’s last shipment to Ukraine was made about 10 months ago. Pagella Politica, an Italian fact-checking outlet, found that deliveries authorized under earlier packages continued during 2026, even though no new package had been approved.

articles.title: Russia’s Newest “Jamming-Resistant” Cruise Missile Crashes in Ukraine
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Newest “Jamming-Resistant” Cruise Missile Crashes in Ukraine
Russia’s latest upgraded Geran-5 K5-K cruise missile, designed to navigate without satellite signals and resist electronic warfare, has crashed in Ukraine’s Odesa region, with newly released photographs showing the advanced weapon lying largely intact in an open field.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on October 27, the missile, bearing serial number ANS-3031, was discovered following a Russian attack. The circumstances surrounding its fall remain unclear, with no confirmation of whether it was intercepted by Ukrainian air defenses, disrupted by electronic warfare, or brought down by a technical malfunction.
The photographs reveal the redesigned fuselage of the Geran-5 K5-K, one of Russia’s newest jet-powered strike weapons, which reportedly entered combat use in late September 2026.
Unlike earlier versions, the upgraded missile features smaller swept-back wings, a modified tail section, and a turbojet engine integrated directly into its fuselage rather than mounted externally. One of its most significant upgrades is an autonomous optical navigation system designed to operate without satellite signals.
According to Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, the system compares images of the terrain below with stored reference data, allowing the missile to adjust its flight path even when satellite navigation is unavailable or disrupted by electronic warfare.
This technology is intended to make the weapon more resistant to Ukrainian electronic warfare systems, which are widely used to interfere with Russian drones and missiles.
Russian developers are reportedly seeking to increase the upgraded missile’s speed to as much as 900 km/h (559 mph), although it remains unclear whether the latest version has achieved that capability.
Russia first deployed the original Geran-5 against Ukraine in January 2026. Ukrainian military intelligence identified the weapon as a turbojet-powered cruise missile with a conventional aerodynamic configuration resembling Iran’s Karrar drone.
The original Geran-5 measures approximately 6.5 meters in length, has a wingspan of 3.2 meters, and carries a warhead weighing around 90 kilograms. Its reported operational range reaches approximately 1,000 kilometers, with cruising speeds between 450 and 600 km/h.
Earlier, Russia’s Alabuga plant in Tatarstan reportedly reached a production capacity of over 3,500 Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones per month, alongside more than 3,000 Shahed-type drones, with support from Chinese technology and components.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv retaking territory, Zelenskyy says, as Nordic leaders urge Putin to end the conflict
articles.body:
- Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukrainian forces are retaking territory through a series of offensives, adding Kyiv’s battlefield position was the strongest it had been in some time. The Ukrainian president, citing a report by senior commanders, noted for the first time the “Veles” operation using pipelines in Ukraine’s northeast. He also referred to an air assault operation in eastern Ukraine and the “Vivaldi” operation further to the north, designed to prevent Russian advances in key areas.
- The leaders of Finland and Norway phoned Russian president Vladimir Putin on Tuesday to urge him to end the war in Ukraine. The call by Finnish president Alexander Stubb and Norwegian prime minister Jonas Gahr Stoere was an attempt to influence the diplomatic process after US president Donald Trump stunned allies by agreeing to buy Russian diesel, plunging ties with Ukraine to their lowest point in 18 months.
- While a localised ceasefire appears to holding in Ukraine’s south, Russian strikes damaged a university campus and Kyiv’s important Southern Bridge overnight, in what Zelenskyy described as “a serious escalation” against Ukrainian logistics. A Ukrainian military source told Reuters that Russia had hit the bridge with four Iskander ballistic missiles. Zelenskyy said energy facilities, logistics and infrastructure in 10 other regions had also been attacked overnight.
- Kyiv plans to allocate 1 billion hryvnias ($22 million) to build water crossings over the River Dnipro that divides the capital into two parts, the city’s mayor has said, as Russia escalates its attacks on bridges.
- Romanian president Nicusor Dan has called an alleged Russian sabotage plot last month a “grave violation” of the Nato member’s sovereignty and security. Dan’s remarks on Tuesday came a day after the Romanian intelligence service said it identified a Russia-coordinated “sabotage network” linked to a fire in central Brasov County last month, which damaged the premises of several commercial entities. Three foreign nationals – two Belarusians and one Ukrainian, all residing in EU countries – were being investigated in connection with the fire. Romania’s foreign ministry said on Tuesday it had summoned Russia’s ambassador in Bucharest. The Russian embassy in Romania said its ambassador rejected the “baseless” accusations.
- France has temporarily relocated a maritime patrol aircraft to Romania to help identify navigation dangers and bolster the protection of critical energy infrastructure in the Black Sea. At least eight cargo ships have been hit near the coast Romania and Bulgaria in the past three weeks, with about 34 sailors reported dead or missing. Romania’s defence ministry said on Tuesday the purpose is “to identify dangers to navigation and increase the ability to protect critical infrastructure in Romania’s exclusive economic zone”.
- Poland will host a maintenance centre for the US-made Patriot air-defence system. The centre in Poland will be the only one outside the US, deputy defence minister Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said on social media. Poland, a Nato member bordering Ukraine, serves as a major logistics hub for military aid sent by Kyiv’s allies. Patriot interceptor missiles are regarded as among Ukraine’s most important air-defence assets as it seeks to repel escalating Russian missile and drone attacks.
- Pope Leo XIV’s chief almsgiver, Monsignor Luis Marín de San Martín, on Tuesday began a three-day visit to Ukraine and was bringing several trucks worth of winter clothes, blankets and food to Kyiv for distribution. Marín de San Martín was planning to visit the capital, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro and Fastiv, Vatican News said. Leo had called for a ceasefire and the delivery of food and medicine in Oleshky, and the safe and voluntary evacuation of its people during a phone calls with Putin and Zelenskyy.

articles.title: Ethiopia receives its first Russian-made Su-35 fighter jets
articles.body:
- Ethiopia has received its first 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets, a year ahead of schedule, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said on Oct. 28.
- Abiy said Ethiopia will also receive four S-400 air defense batteries but did not disclose the deal’s value or delivery timeline.
Ethiopia has taken delivery of its first 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets and will also receive four batteries of the S-400 long-range air defense system, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said on social media on Oct. 28.
Abiy said the jets arrived under an earlier agreement with the Russian government and a year ahead of the agreed schedule, and he thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for the early delivery. He did not disclose the value of the deal, its terms, or when the S-400 batteries will arrive, Addis Standard reported.
“In accordance with our prior agreement with the Russian government, we have today taken delivery of the first twelve Su-35 4++ Generation fighter jets,” said Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
The announcement came while Abiy was in Russia for the third Russia-Africa Summit, according to Ethiopian state broadcaster Fana Media Corporation, which reported that he witnessed the official handover of the aircraft. Abiy described the purchase as a major boost to the defense forces and said it puts Ethiopia in the lead among Sub-Saharan African nations.
The Su-35 is Russia’s most advanced fighter in export service after the Su-57. It is a single-seat, twin-engine multirole jet built for both air combat and ground attack, with thrust-vectoring engines that let it maneuver sharply and a long-range Irbis-E radar. Sukhoi calls it a “4++ generation” aircraft, meaning a heavily upgraded fourth-generation design that stops short of the stealth features of fifth-generation fighters.
The S-400 is a long-range surface-to-air missile system designed to shoot down aircraft and some missiles. A battery typically includes radars, a command post and several launcher vehicles.
Ethiopia’s interest in the Su-35 first surfaced a year ago. In October 2025, a hacker group called Black Mirror published internal files from Russian state defense conglomerate Rostec that listed Ethiopia as having signed a contract for six Su-35s, alongside larger orders for Iran and Algeria. Neither Rostec nor the Ethiopian government commented at the time. The 12 jets Abiy announced are double the number in the leaked documents, and his description of them as the “first” twelve suggests more could follow, though he did not say how many Ethiopia has ordered in total.
The new jets will join an air force that has flown Russian Sukhoi fighters for more than 25 years. Ethiopia received Su-27s in the late 1990s and used them in its 1998 to 2000 border war with Eritrea. In January 2024, it inducted Su-30K fighters, believed to come from a batch originally built for the Indian Air Force, along with Turkish Akinci drones.
Only a handful of countries have received the Su-35 for export. China took delivery of 24 aircraft between 2016 and 2018, and Algeria received its first units in March 2025, Army Recognition reported. The S-400 is in service with China, India and Turkey, and Turkey’s purchase led the United States to impose sanctions on its defense procurement agency in 2020 under a law targeting significant arms deals with Russia.
Tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea have risen this year, and Russia has offered to host talks between the two countries, Addis Standard reported. Abiy said the new equipment would allow Ethiopia to deter aggression and support regional stability.

articles.title: Russian satellites help Iran's allies strike Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Russian satellites help Iran's allies strike Saudi Arabia
Iranian-backed militias carried out a precision strike last month, hitting the pumping stations of Saudi Arabia’s most important oil pipeline. Days later, another attack hit a Saudi military air base, damaging an Italian fighter jet inside a hangar.
Crucial to the strikes' success was what was happening in the skies overhead: For days beforehand, a constellation of Russian spy satellites converged over the pipeline and the air base to gather intelligence.
A private geospatial intelligence firm said it examined 40 missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia by Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen and militias in Iraq between July 1 and Oct. 19. In every case, the firm found the same pattern of Russian government and military satellites orbiting above the areas for days before and after.
"What we found is a 100% match" between the satellite activities and strikes, said Nawaf Obaid, founder of Geneva-based AURORAH Geosignal Intelligence.
The findings illustrate how Russia is believed to be helping Iran and its allies in the region target Saudi Arabia’s oil and military infrastructure in attacks that have helped raise global energy prices.
Three officials, including one from Saudi Arabia and another in the top ranks of the Houthis, as well as a private intelligence analyst, told The Associated Press that the Houthis and other Iranian allies have benefited from Russian intelligence, as well as Chinese capabilities. Iranian advisers in the field analyzed and transferred the intelligence to their allies, according to AP reporting.
The Saudi Foreign Ministry’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, Rayed Krimly, told reporters last week that Iran and the Houthis receive intelligence from "elements in Russia and China, even commercial elements sometimes."
"We do discuss these matters regularly with China and Russia, and we will continue to do so," he said.
Russian officials had no immediate comment when asked about the allegations, including AURORAH’s findings.
Russia and Iran have a longstanding military cooperation arrangement, including transferring drone technology. While Russia has not been directly involved in the wars in the region, U.S. and European officials have said Russia has shared intelligence with Iran.
Iranian-backed groups were able to carry out pinpoint strikes 
On the morning of Sept. 10, multiple drone strikes from Iraq hit three critical pumping stations along Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, immediately interrupting the flow of oil. The 1,200-kilometer (746-mile) pipeline across the kingdom has been a vital alternative route for getting its crude to market amid Iran’s attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
The pumping stations are vital to moving oil through the pipeline, which rises more than 1,100 meters (3,608 feet) in altitude as it goes from eastern Saudi Arabia across the Najd Plateau then back down to the kingdom’s western coast on the Red Sea, said Obaid, a fellow at King’s College Department of War Studies who also served as an adviser to various Saudi officials from 2004 to 2016.
"This is where the militias out of Iraq decided to strike," he said.
Beginning in July, his firm observed 11 of Russia’s Cosmos 2600 series satellites concentrating on those three sections of the pipeline. Flybys increased in the weeks leading up to the attacks and in the hours around the strikes, showing reconnaissance before and after, he said.
A week later, King Fahd Air Base in Taif, Saudi Arabia, was hit with multiple projectiles fired by the Iranian-backed Houthis. Along with hangars at the base, an Italian air force Eurofighter Typhoon jet was damaged, according to the Italian Defense Ministry. The Italian military has had assets deployed in Saudi Arabia for years as part of the U.S.-led coalition’s campaigns in Iraq and Syria.
In both those cases, Obaid's firm monitored a 50% increase in the number of Russian satellites orbiting above the targets during a 72-hour period before and after the strikes, compared with July.
Notably, the Taif attack precisely hit the Italian warplane rather than Saudi ones stationed at the same base, suggesting "highly specialized intelligence support that the Houthis and Iranians simply don’t have," Obaid said.
The Houthis have warned foreign powers not to help Saudi Arabia.
A clear pattern of satellites is visible 
AURORAH used open-source information as well as other intelligence sources to identify 72 Russian reconnaissance satellites out of more than 11,000 spacecraft orbiting the Earth, Obaid said. It then tracked their trajectories and maneuvers while comparing them to military activity on the ground.
The firm has not intercepted actual transmission of intelligence to Iran or its allies, Obaid said. Instead, the firm has established a definitive pattern of Russian satellite positions and reconnaissance activity around strategic targets ahead of strikes, indicating that intelligence is being collected and transferred for Houthi and Iraqi militia targeting, he said.
Obaid said the same satellite patterns also occurred in connection with Iranian strikes on U.S. bases in the Middle East during the U.S.-Iran war that began in February.
“That is the fundamental transformation in the regional military balance: The intelligence system behind the weapon is becoming as important as the weapon itself,” he said.
Adam Marsh, vice president of technological solutions at California-based Leolabs, an orbital intelligence firm, said the massing of satellites is what one would expect to see for purposes of collecting intelligence. The Russians can deny they are doing it, he said, but he noted there is only a general policy and no regulatory body: “How would you stop anybody?”
Satellite intelligence has also helped Houthis in their fight inside Yemen 
An official briefed on investigations in Saudi Arabia into recent attacks said intelligence showed that Russian satellites had helped Houthis and Iraqi militias strike sensitive targets, including the pumping stations on the East-West Pipeline. The official spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to journalists.
The satellites also helped strikes by Iran in March on Saudi Arabia’s Prince Sultan Air Base, where a U.S. surveillance aircraft was severely damaged, and on a CIA unit inside the U.S. Embassy complex in Riyadh, the official said.
The investigations found that missiles and drones used by the Houthis in their strikes had Russian- and Chinese-made components, the official said.
Russian satellite intelligence has also helped the Houthis in the dramatic advances they made against Saudi-backed opponents in Yemen’s civil war, according to Obaid and a Houthi leader.
AURORAH identified satellite configurations over targets in connection to an Oct. 15 Houthi strike on the presidential palace in Yemen’s southern port city of Aden and a nearby command center used by the Saudi-led coalition, as well as a strike on a government recruitment center in the province of Shabwa that killed 75 new recruits, Obaid said.
Iranian advisers on the ground in Yemen have been providing the rebels with data based on Russian satellite intelligence to help in targeting, a senior Houthi leader told the AP. The leader spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the confidential role of the advisers.
Mzahem Alsaloum, a security analyst who has followed Iranian-backed groups for nearly a decade and now runs a private intelligence firm, said the advisers use Russian spy satellite information to provide Iranians with target lists and operational information.
The Houthi leader also said the Iranians provided the rebels with more advanced equipment, including systems for piloting drones and for helping missiles evade air defenses.
The equipment was developed by the Iranians, bought commercially or provided by Russia and China, he said, though he did not know whether those countries were aware the equipment was being used in the Yemen war.

articles.title: Oleshky truce appears to hold as two European leaders have ‘frank’ call with Putin
articles.body:
A local ceasefire in a southern Ukrainian city under Russian occupation appeared to be holding on Tuesday, with both sides ceasing drone attacks ahead of an apparent evacuation of about 2,000 trapped and desperate civilians.
The temporary truce began at 3am in Russian-controlled Oleshky. The city sits on the Dnipro River and is about 3 miles (5km) from Kherson, a larger city on the opposite bank. Ukrainian troops recaptured Kherson in autumn 2022.
Witnesses reported that the deadly frontline across the river was quiet for the first time in four years. The pause in fighting is due to last until 11pm on Sunday, Ukrainian officials said, and represents a significant if limited moment of de-escalation.
Finland’s president, Alexander Stubb, and Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, held what they described as a “frank and substantive” phone call with Vladimir Putin about efforts to end the war in Ukraine. Støre indicated afterwards that big differences remained.
The two Nordic leaders said the call – a rare instance of direct contact between Putin and western leaders – was linked to upcoming talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US, expected to take place in Abu Dhabi next month.
The ceasefire in Oleshky appears to be an attempt by the Kremlin to curry favour with Donald Trump before the trilateral meeting and next week’s US midterm elections. The first lady, Melania Trump, requested the humanitarian mission, and in a post on X said it was brought forward by two days to allow the delivery of critical aid.
Its geographical scope had been extended beyond Oleshky “within the Kherson region”, she added, to provide safe passage for convoys. Calls for a ceasefire were also issued by Pope Leo, the United Nations, EU officials and the Council of Europe.
Between 1,500 and 2,000 people in the city have been living under a complete blockade by Russia. The last delivery of food to stores was in May, and many people are now starving and eating weeds. The Ukrainian military has airdropped food using drones but locals say Russian security forces detain anyone who takes it.
Russian soldiers have mined roads and use ruined buildings to coordinate round-the-clock strikes against Kherson. Some Oleshky residents have managed to escape, walking or cycling past bodies lying on the street and the burnt-out shells of vehicles.
Ukrainian observers say the Kremlin is planning a major propaganda tour this week in which Kyiv is blamed for Oleshky’s destruction. Trump-supporting US media channels have been invited to witness the evacuation, in which buses will take residents to occupied Crimea and Russia.
Ksenia Arkhipova, who fled the city in 2022 and now, as a volunteer, helps others leave, said some residents have told her they fear Russian officials may “filter out” evacuees with pro-Ukraine views.
“People say they are genuinely afraid that the Russians will check their phones and look for evidence of Ukrainian relatives or ties to the Armed Forces of Ukraine – something they have done repeatedly in other occupied territories,” Arkhipova told the Associated Press.
The ceasefire does not extend to other parts of Ukraine. Overnight, Russia bombarded Kyiv with drones and ballistic missiles, killing at least one person and injuring 15. It hit a university campus, wounding students, as well as a bridge over the Dnipro and metro infrastructure. Ten other regions came under fire.
The bridge remains closed to traffic, but some commuters walked across it to get to work. Writing on social media, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia “must stop dragging out this war” and said he welcomed European attempts to end it.
He said Stubb and Støre had briefed him on their call with Putin. “Alex and Jonas clearly conveyed to the Russian leadership the need for genuine steps towards de-escalation, particularly when it comes to our energy sector and infrastructure,” Zelenskyy wrote.
The Finnish-Norwegian initiative comes amid growing efforts by some European nations to establish a direct channel of communication with Moscow and secure a stronger European voice in negotiations. Stubb and Støre said they took part in the call as leaders of their respective countries and were not speaking on behalf of Europe as a whole.
European governments remain divided over whether direct engagement with Putin is worthwhile, given Russia’s maximalist demands remain stubbornly unchanged. There is little agreement on who should lead such talks. Stubb is seen by some EU officials as a candidate.
The divisions were laid bare shortly after news of the call emerged, when Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, criticised the move. “I am very sceptical about this independent initiative by Norway and Finland. It was not agreed with any of us,” Frederiksen said.
She added: “I see no signs that Russia wants peace with Europe – neither in the hybrid warfare it wages every day, nor in Ukraine, where brutal and aggressive strikes continue daily, claiming many lives.”
Russia’s foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, said the Europeans had offered “nothing new”, and were simply trying to insert themselves in the negotiation process.
This month Putin said he was willing to resume peace talks, but only on Russia’s hardline terms. They include the handover of the entire eastern Donbas region, including parts Russia has been unable to seize since 2014, as well as further territory in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia provinces.
Last week Zelenskyy said he was open to a peace agreement that would freeze the war along the current frontlines. “Yes, we are ready to stop this war as soon as possible,” he said in an interview with ABC News. He made clear that Ukraine would not recognise land seized and occupied by Russia as Russian.

articles.title: Kyiv approves alternative Dnipro crossings after Russian strikes on bridges
articles.body:
People cross the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River on foot after a Russian missile strike damaged it. Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 27, 2026 (The Kyiv Independent)
Kyiv City Mayor Vitali Klitschko announced that alternative, temporary river crossings will be created to bridge the Dnipro, after Kyiv's Southern Bridge was struck in a Russian ballistic missile attack in the morning.
"The locations will be determined by the military command and will be coordinated, in particular, by the Kyiv City Military Administration," Klitschko said after a meeting of the city's Capital Defense Council.
Kyiv's Southern Bridge was struck by at least one Russian ballistic missile on the morning of Oct. 27, leaving a large hole in the structure and closing the bridge to both road and rail traffic.
Commuters heading to work from the city's largely residential left bank had to make a half-hour trek across the structure on foot.
The city will provide funding of 1 billion hryvnias (about $22 million) for the project, the mayor said.
