articles.title: US warns Gulf of 'intense' return to Iran war after midterms
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US warns Gulf states to brace for 'intense' Iran war after midterms
The US has warned several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a possible short but intense military campaign against Iran following next week's US midterm elections, according to a report published by The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday.
The warnings, delivered through diplomatic and military channels, come as the US and Israel make preparations for renewed strikes against Iran, potentially targeting the country's nuclear facilities and other critical infrastructure.
US President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on launching another military operation, but is leaning towards a major attack after the 3 November elections, the newspaper reported, citing people familiar with his thinking.
The preparations are intended to give Trump military options while Washington continues to pursue an agreement with Tehran.
The US military is transferring an additional Patriot missile defence system from Texas to Israel, according to flight-tracking data and officials familiar with the deployment.
American forces have also relocated personnel from vulnerable military bases across the Middle East, replenished ammunition stockpiles and prepared bombers and fighter aircraft for potential operations.
An additional aircraft carrier strike group and Marine expeditionary unit are expected to join approximately 20 American warships already operating in the region next month, although some vessels could be withdrawn.
Israel has also reportedly identified targets and prepared plans for another military offensive, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu continuing to advocate further strikes against Iran.
The White House declined to discuss the reported preparations.
"President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon," it said.
Trump has previously said he would not attack Iran before the midterm elections.
Speaking at a campaign rally in Texas on Tuesday, he suggested that further developments involving Iran could follow within weeks.
"You'll see Iran in a couple of weeks, if you don't mind," Trump said.
Gulf states face renewed threat
The reported preparations come as Gulf governments attempt to prevent another regional war while confronting the prospect of Iranian retaliation against their territory.
Iran has warned that further American or Israeli attacks would provoke strikes against economic and military targets across the region.
During the previous phase of the war, Iranian missiles and drones targeted American military facilities, diplomatic installations, energy infrastructure and airports in Gulf countries.
Another confrontation could expose Gulf states to renewed attacks at a time when Washington and its regional allies are attempting to replenish missile defence systems depleted during earlier fighting.
Despite extensive American and Israeli bombardment, Iran retains substantial missile capabilities and has reportedly been rebuilding its military arsenal and air defences.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on 28 February, with Iranian responding with attacks on what it said were US facilities in the region and closing the Strait of Hormuz.
Washington subsequently intensified economic pressure through sanctions and a naval blockade that have severely restricted Iranian oil exports and international trade.
Renewed diplomatic efforts
The prospect of renewed attacks comes amid diplomatic efforts by regional governments to secure an agreement between Washington and Tehran.
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have recently participated in high-level consultations with Iranian officials, while other regional mediators have attempted to revive negotiations over Iran's nuclear programme.
However, the talks have made little progress, with Washington insisting on restrictions on Iran's nuclear activities and Tehran maintaining its own conditions for negotiations.
The International Atomic Energy Agency said on Tuesday that it had identified no evidence of reconstruction at Iranian nuclear facilities damaged during previous American and Israeli attacks.
However, agency chief Rafael Grossi warned that inspectors had been unable to access the damaged sites or verify the status of Iran's nuclear material.
Analysts have also questioned whether further military action would compel Tehran to make concessions, warning that renewed attacks could instead strengthen Iran's determination to rebuild its military capabilities.
The reported American preparations therefore leave Gulf governments confronting the possibility of another major regional conflict, even as diplomatic efforts to prevent renewed fighting continue.

articles.title: Ukrainian intelligence says Russia’s missile makers use gear from seven countries—and the Chinese machines run on European, Japanese, and Taiwanese parts
articles.body:
Machine tools and other equipment from seven countries, led by China, work at Russian plants that make ballistic missiles and their components, Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) said on 26 October. The 30 items are a small slice of HUR’s War&Sanctions portal, which lists 1,698 machine tools at 223 Russian plants.
Seventeen of the 30 were made outside China, in Germany, Taiwan, the US, Türkiye, Switzerland, and Italy. One of HUR’s proposals reaches past Russia and China, to the firms that supply parts for Chinese machine tools. The list comes two weeks after the EU blacklisted 1,569 Russian arms suppliers and executives. More than half of those listings hit the ballistic missile supply chain, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said. Sanctioning a company, though, does not stop the machines in its workshops.
A Chinese machine at the Iskander plant
HUR’s statement leads with a GX-650 five-axis machining center made by China’s Hyper Machine Tool. Such computer-controlled machines cut complex metal parts from several angles. HUR said it works at the Votkinsk Plant, which the agency described as the maker of 9M723 missiles for the Iskander-M system and the missile section of the Kh-47M2 Kinzhal, an air-launched ballistic missile.
Kinzhal is 90% identical to Iskander-M: Ukraine’s intelligence identifies 58 companies in production chain
HUR has flagged Votkinsk before. In November 2025, it published hackathon findings showing that Russian companies supplied Chinese and Taiwanese machine tools to the plant after the full-scale invasion began.
Chinese Shtral turning and milling centers work at PEMZ Molot, which builds electronics units for Iskander-M missiles, according to HUR’s statement. At UPKB Detal, which makes altimeters for hypersonic Zircon cruise missiles, HUR found measuring equipment from Germany’s Rohde & Schwarz.
The portal entries paint a broader picture. Only four of the 30 entries list a ballistic missile among the plant’s weapons. Most of the rest list cruise missiles, glide-bomb kits, guided artillery shells, or Geran-2 attack drones. HUR did not publish its evidence, though the portal says partner agencies can request it.
Foreign parts inside Chinese machines
Russian plants use the equipment to make missiles and parts such as altimeters, control surfaces, and gyroscopes, HUR said. The agency noted a growing number of Chinese machine tools, including five-axis models. According to HUR, those Chinese machines contain European, Japanese, and Taiwanese components, from numerical control systems to precision spindles and bearings. In HUR’s assessment, Russia still cannot replace equipment from leading foreign makers with its own.

- Iskander Russia fired at Kyiv Oblast in July held 62 American parts. Ukraine has now named more than 100 Russian ballistics producers and wants its allies to sanction all of them
- Russian plant supplying components for Iskander missiles reportedly struck by Ukrainian Storm Shadow missiles

articles.title: US chooses Poland to host service facility for Patriot missiles
articles.body:

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
The United States has chosen Poland to host a new centre for servicing and maintaining missiles used in Patriot air defence systems, in a decision described as “historic” by both Washington and Warsaw. It was chosen ahead of bids from four other European countries.
The new centre, the first of its kind ot be located outside the US itself, will “dramatically shorten turnaround times and further secure critical supply lines”, said the US Department of War, announcing the decision on Tuesday.
Undersecretary of War Michael P. Duffey added that the choice of a country on NATO’s eastern front “sends a clear message [that] the Alliance is united, serious about deterrence, and ready to back our words with action”.
Poland Selected to Host Historic PAC-3 Missile Maintenance Facility, Strengthening Allied Burden-Sharing and Transatlantic Security – U.S. Department of War – Release | @DeptofWar https://t.co/2caqADRRx8
— US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) October 27, 2026
The decision was welcomed by Polish leaders, with defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz saying that it shows “Poland is a trusted ally and holds an extremely important place on the map of global security”.
His deputy minister, Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, said that Poland was chosen ahead of rival bids from Germany, the Netherlands and Norway to host the facility. However, US ambassador to Poland Thomas Rose indicated that Sweden, not Norway, was the fourth candidate.
Kosiniak-Kamysz and Sobkowiak-Czarnecka both pointed to the role President Karol Nawrocki had played in securing the deal. On many issues, the government is in conflict with the opposition-aligned president, but the two sides worked together on the Patriot bid.
Historyczna decyzja! Centrum serwisowania pocisków PAC-3 do systemów Patriot powstanie w Polsce! 🇵🇱
O europejską lokalizację tej inwestycji rywalizowały cztery państwa, obok Polski – Niemcy, Holandia i Norwegia. Już na etapie składania wniosków polska oferta została oceniona… pic.twitter.com/wUgFhzlzUk
— Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) October 27, 2026
Nawrocki, a conservative, is a close ally of his US counterpart, Donald Trump. The Polish president’s national security advisor, Bartosz Grodecki, claimed that it was “thanks to a conversation between” the two presidents that the new Patriot servicing centre was being established in Poland.
The head of Nawrocki’s foreign policy office, Marcin Przydacz, meanwhile, thanked Washington for choosing Poland to host the new centre.
“The Polish-American alliance and the good atmosphere in relations once again yield results,” he declared. “We can see what positive effects the President’s activity brings for Poland.”
Poland is one of a number of European countries that operate Patriot air defence systems. Others include Germany, Greece, the Netherlands, Romania, Sweden and Ukraine.
The new centre will service the PAC-3 missiles used in Patriot batteries. The competition to host the facility was announced in July, with the selection made by the US government in conjunction with American defence giant Lockheed Martin, the producer of missiles.
In its press release, the Pentagon emphasised that, although Poland would host the new centre, its work would “be underpinned by robust, transatlantic industrial cooperation, with critical supply chain integration led by Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden”.
Sweden will deploy Patriot air defence systems and around 100 accompanying military personnel to Poland later this year to protect the NATO logistics hub in the city of Rzeszów, which is the main conduit for aid to Ukraine https://t.co/cq9p7OVO7E
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 6, 2026
Global demand for Patriot systems has risen significantly, with the United States expending at least 1,500 interceptors in its war with Iran, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Patriot systems have also been crucial in Ukraine’s defence against Russian ballistic missile attacks, although Ukraine’s supply of missiles is now almost entirely exhausted.
After Trump recently suggested that he would authorise Ukraine to produce its own missiles, Poland offered to host any such factory, to ensure its security. However, today’s announcement concerns a site for maintaining and servicing, rather than producing, the missiles.
Poland has proposed that, if the United States grants Ukraine permission to produce its own missiles for Patriot air-defence systems, the facility could be located on Polish territory to ensure its security https://t.co/jaQng5wtGg
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 28, 2026
The decision cements Poland’s position as one of Washington’s most important security partners in Europe. War secretary Pete Hegseth has praised Poland as a “model ally”, noting that it has for years met NATO’s defence spending targets, unlike many other member states.
Poland has also been a significant customer for US defence firms. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was NATO’s biggest arms importer, with 44% of the equipment it purchased coming from American suppliers.
Last year, Poland signed a $2 billion deal for the US to provide logistical support and training for Patriot systems. This year, it was announced that Polish state defence group PGZ would become the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles.
Poland will become the first country in Europe to produce cruise missiles developed by US defence firm Anduril Industries
The agreement will "transform the continent's defence industry", claims Anduril https://t.co/LPJnwOLfp2
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026
Warsaw is also currently lobbying for a new permanent US military base to be established in Poland, with the government and the president once again putting aside their differences to promote the idea.
Last month, Nawrocki claimed that the proposed base, which he said would be called “Fort Trump”, was “confirmed”. However, Washington has not publicly announced any final decision.

articles.title: Trump is in a corner and likely to lash out at Iran again. Here’s how to avert that disaster | Simon Tisdall
articles.body:
As another Iran catastrophe looms, one question matters more than any other: how to stop it before it’s too late? Whatever the eventual outcome of Israel’s election and next week’s US midterm polls, Donald Trump, playing the Lone Ranger, and Benjamin Netanyahu, his badass Tonto, appear hell-bent on resuming the illegal war of choice they began in June last year and expanded in February. Like a Shakespearean tragedy moving inexorably to a bloody denouement, the worst is yet to come. And yet three things seem certain: the US and Israel will again fail to totally destroy Iran’s largely hypothetical nuclear capabilities; its regime will survive; and millions of ordinary people, there and around the world, will pay the price for this unjustified, reckless aggression.
Ducking and weaving, Trump is desperate to dodge the blame for the Republicans’ anticipated midterm meltdown, largely triggered by war-related fuel and consumer price inflation. He claimed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries were responsible, but that didn’t wash. He cut a treacherous diesel deal with Vladimir Putin but, as usual, Russia’s smirking mafioso conned him. He urged US allies to tap their strategic reserves but, unsurprisingly, vilified and sidelined European leaders, who view his war as an unmitigated disaster and declined to bail him out. Trump also reportedly rebuffed last-gasp, electorally driven pressure from Netanyahu to hit Iran this month, fearful it would unleash a Democratic tsunami.
Yet once the midterm polls close, and whatever the results, all these considerations fall away. What voters think will no longer matter to Trump. At that point, he can do more or less what he wants, in foreign and defence policy, for his final two years. And what he wants has little to do with imaginary Iranian nukes, a democratic uprising in Tehran, or any of his other bogus justifications for waging war. Trump will be free to do what he does best: vendetta politics. Iran’s greatest sin is to have defied the imperial will. He wanted an easy Venezuela-style, regime-altering victory (and sweetheart oil deals). What he got was a middle digit, burnt fingers and a forever war. Just as he vengefully pursues opponents at home, so he now victimises Iranians. It’s not rational or ideological. Like everything with Trump, ultimately it’s personal.
Netanyahu’s reasons for wanting another bash are thoroughly dishonourable too, but in a different way. Given his myriad, chronic failures before and after the 2023 Hamas massacres, his trashing of Israel’s international reputation by his criminal actions in Gaza and Lebanon, and his Trump-ish slide into bigoted, ultra-nationalist authoritarianism, Netanyahu is fighting for his job and, potentially, his freedom. He insists, despite his record, that only he can ensure Israel’s security. He suggests, outrageously, that opposition victory could pave the way for Israel’s destruction in a second, nuclear Holocaust. Israel’s military chiefs suspect he may restart the Iran war in order to dominate and manipulate the inevitable post-election coalition talks – hoping to stay in power and out of jail.
The likely, mortifying consequences of a renewed US-Israel onslaught after 3 November should be fully understood. For starters, the price of oil will spike again, perhaps to unprecedented levels, negatively affecting people all around the world. Pentagon officials, possibly peddling disinformation, suggest Iran is preparing to retaliate with missile and drone attacks against Saudi and other Gulf oil refineries, infrastructure and underwater internet cables, while reinforcing blockades of the strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea’s Bab al-Mandab strait. The impact on international energy supplies, transportation and international trade generally could be far worse than last spring.
Trump reportedly plans a shock-and-awe, time-limited assault – primarily on the mountain complex where Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium is supposedly stored, plus its missile bases and energy grid. If this sounds familiar, it is. Trump’s chief gunslinger, Pete Hegseth, and his air-force cowboys claim to have destroyed many of these targets already, some more than once. Total success will probably elude them again. What’s more likely is that the war’s duration will lengthen, and more Iranian civilians will suffer the fate of over 100 schoolgirls killed in a Tomahawk missile strike in Minab in February. For that atrocity and others, Trump and Hegseth have never admitted responsibility.
Other foreseeable consequences include: the spread of related conflicts, involving Iranian allies and proxy militias, to Yemen, Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Lebanon; attacks on US embassies and personnel from Jordan to Kuwait; intensified, opportunistic settler violence and land grabs in the West Bank; stepped-up Iranian freelance assassination and sabotage operations in Europe; further undermining of US and Israeli democracy from deliberate obstruction of war-zone accountability, official cover-ups and blatant lying, and restrictions on independent media reporting; another hugely damaging split between Washington and its reluctant European allies; and another geopolitical free lunch for the west’s anti-democratic challengers, Russia and China.
Here are two more questions. By what right does the US, in particular, presume to behave in this way? Forget, if you can, Trump and Netanyahu. What does the American public (or at least, those who vote Republican) say? Have they not learned by now, after so many disastrous interventions that the world does not want, and does not need, to be saved by the US? In the age of Maga, this vulgar exceptionalism has surely had its day. Second, reformulated question: how may this looming catastrophe be prevented? Resumed warfare, leading to a wider, globally destabilising conflagration, is not inevitable. But urgent action is necessary now.
A talks process, mediated by Qatar, though neglected and boycotted by the White House, has not completely collapsed. Negotiations could yet produce viable outcomes if given a chance, Badr Albusaidi, Oman’s foreign minister, told the Guardian this week. A longer-term solution, he suggested, could be a non-aggression pact involving all six Gulf states, plus Iran and Iraq, acting on the premise that they, not the US, would be the primary, joint providers of future regional security. As Albusaidi spoke, top officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey were in Tehran on a last-ditch mission to pre-empt resumed hostilities. All power to them. At least they’re trying.
It would be reassuring to think Trump and Netanyahu are listening. But the bottom line is that, for their different reasons, both men probably want this war. A firm, united course of rapid, preventive action is required to head them off. Britain, its European allies and like-minded governments took a tentative, defiant step in Istanbul last weekend, urging diplomacy over violence. Now they and all the world’s democracies must stand as one and, in a formal demarche, tell the US and Israel they risk a permanent rupture with immediate and long-term negative economic, diplomatic, commercial, military and security consequences if they ignore global opinion and go to war again.
Trump is not king of the world. And Netanyahu cannot do as he likes with impunity. It’s high time they were told.
- Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

articles.title: Ukraine receives 12 Patriot missiles per month from US, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Ukraine has received an average of 12 Patriot interceptor missiles per month from the U.S. throughout 2026, President Volodymyr Zelensky told journalist on Oct. 27 at a closed-door press briefing.
Ukraine needs to intercept around 150 Russian ballistic missiles per month but receives about 150 Patriot missiles from the U.S. annually, according to Zelensky.
The president said some European countries have agreed to provide additional missiles from their stockpiles, but the transfers require approval from Washington. Zelensky pointed to documents awaiting action by U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
"We want the Americans to start signing off on the supply of antiballistic missiles – interceptor missiles – to Ukraine from the countries we've reached agreements with. Because without Hegseth's signature, it's simply impossible," Zelensky said.
Zelsnky said on Oct. 26 that Kyiv has been waiting nearly a month for Hegseth to approve missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems. Ukrainian officials have described the delays and disruptions as an example of political pressure from Washington that could put civilian lives at risk.
Ukraine obtains Patriot interceptors through several channels, including NATO's Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), a mechanism through which Kyiv's allies fund weapons purchases from the United States.
The shortage also affects missiles for NASAMS air defense systems, which Ukraine receives through the PURL initiative.
Zelensky also said he had asked U.S. President Donald Trump for a special package of interceptor missiles ahead of winter during a meeting in New York on Sept. 22. Trump promised to make efforts to secure the missiles, Zelensky said, but noted that the U.S. also needed them for their own defense.
"These are the circumstances I live in today: every week, we have to put together new packages, find new missiles, and secure new air defenses. We need them every day to save the lives of our people from Russian ballistic missiles," Zelensky said.
According to Zelensky, Russia has launched over 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region since Oct. 14.
Ukraine has also recently experienced repeated disruptions to its early-warning systems for incoming Russian ballistic missiles, which rely on U.S. intelligence. American officials have attributed the outages, which have occurred several times in the past, to "bad weather conditions."
Zelensky added that the war in the Middle East has reduced military and financial support for Ukraine, making it more difficult for Kyiv to secure the air defense supplies needed to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.
"The war in the Middle East is having a negative impact on the whole world. The energy challenges around the world are caused exclusively by the Strait of Hormuz. All the other challenges are also affecting Ukraine. The military and financial support Ukraine receives has definitely declined because of the war in the Middle East," he said.

“Every support package is an opportunity to protect people’s lives,” Zelensky said Monday.
Ukraine seeks Patriot interceptors from other partners
With US authorization still pending, Ukraine is pursuing additional interceptor supplies from European countries and other partners.
Zelensky said Monday that Ukrainian officials were working through several channels to secure PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles, both used by Patriot air defense systems.
“We are working on several tracks – with the US, Europe, and other partners that have stocks of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles,” he said.
“Conversations with other countries are also ongoing.”
The president said preparations were underway for the next meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, known as the Ramstein format, expected in November.

articles.title: F-16 Jets to Add Startup Castelion’s Hypersonic ‘Blackbeard’ Missile
articles.body:
The Air Force has awarded Castelion, a venture capital-backed defense startup founded in 2022, a contract to integrate its hypersonic Blackbeard missile onto the F-16 Fighting Falcon.
The announcement, which came from the company via social media on Oct. 26, marks a major advancement in the Air Force’s work on hypersonic munitions.
Neither the Air Force Research Laboratory, which awarded the contract, nor Castelion immediately responded to a request for comment.
The same day, the service awarded a $694 million contract to Lockheed Martin, a longtime defense prime, to begin production of the hypersonic Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported.
The Blackbeard missile has drawn strong interest across the Pentagon, with the Navy pushing to field the rocket-powered, boost-glide strike weapon with a nearly 500-mile strike range on the sea service’s F/A-18 Super Hornet.
Navy Development
The Navy’s Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 23 used the Super Hornet to conduct carriage and separation tests of Blackbeard on Sept. 18 at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Md., which validated the weapon’s compatibility and flightworthiness on the aircraft.
The service selected Blackbeard as the winner in its Multimission Affordable Capacity Effector program, which shifted it to a program of record under framework contract orders of up to $200 million.
The company won a $105 million contract to integrate the missile on the F/A-18 Super Hornet in April.
The MACE initiative sought an affordable hypersonic missile about the size of an AIM-120 AMRAAM air-to-air missile.
In June, the service awarded the company its first production contract, worth $23.4 million, for 50 early operational capability pre-production prototype Blackbeard missiles.
Subsequent delivery orders from the Navy aim to speed up Blackbeard pre-production prototypes to EOC status and field the low-cost hypersonic weapon.
USAF Spending and Development
For its part, the Air Force has spent nearly $21 million to date on Blackbeard research and development, and AFRL added $16.4 million in a September contract modification for the missile.
Those dollars cover development through June 2028 under current spending and contractual agreements.
The USAF contract modification also pursues compatibility with the F-35A.
While the F-35 is the services’ main fifth-generation tactical fighter, the F-16, like the Navy’s workhorse Super Hornet, are workhorse fourth-gen fighters that can carry more munitions without worrying about compromising stealthy characteristics.
The Air Force has more than 600 F-16s in the fleet and recently moved forward with plans to upgrade the decades-old software system for those crucial aircraft, Air & Space Forces Magazine previously reported.
The Big Picture
The Air Force now has a three-pronged approach to hypersonic munitions.
These include Castelion’s Blackbeard, an air-to-air missile; the Lockheed Martin AGM-183A ARRW, a strategic strike-focused, exquisite, long-range hypersonic missile; and the Raytheon/Northrop Grumman Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile, a cruise missile option to strike ground or maritime targets.
ARRW successfully completed booster and All-Up-Round tests and is poised to add terminal seeker and data-link integration for moving-target tracking in its Increment 2 tests. The strategic strike missile is envisioned for the B-52 Stratofortress and B-1B Lancer.
The AHM-4A HACM is built for internal or external carriage and geared for both fighter and bomber use to add high-volume magazine depth to the fleet. The missile achieved milestone flight tests over an undisclosed Australian range in late September, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported. Initial operational delivery of HACMs is slated for 2027.
Additionally, AFRL recently posted a request for white papers on developing a more advanced hypersonic rocket engine for its current and future munitions dubbed the Rotating Detonation Rocket Engine.
If successful, the more affordable, mass-produced engine could extend ranges, increase speed, and up the payload for future hypersonic, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported.

articles.title: Strategic partnership of Poland and Great Britain. Three-Year Defence Cooperation Plan signed.
articles.body:
Strategic partnership of Poland and Great Britain. Three-Year Defence Cooperation Plan signed.
27.10.2026
- The Polish-British alliance has never been as strong as it is today. The agreement we signed, increasing our capabilities and cooperation, is the best example of that. We have signed an agreement on the plan of cooperation in defence. This three-year plan is the result of the Polish-British treaty, signed a few months ago. I am very grateful for this plan of cooperation. It shows our joint involvement: Polish and British soldiers, joint exercises, developing skills. The most important capabilities we are working on are the new technologies, long-range precise strikes, Artificial Intelligence, drones, anti-drone measures, but exercises training our classic capabilities and cooperation in various conditions will be organized based on this defence plan which we have signed today - said the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.
On 27 October 2026, a bilateral meeting took place in Warsaw between the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, and the Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting. The Deputy Minister of National Defence Paweł Zalewski also took part in the talks between the two delegations. The main part of the visit of the British delegation was the signing of the Three-Year Defence Cooperation Plan of the Republic of Poland and the United Kingdom by both ministers.
- Great Britain is an important partner for us when it comes to defence production. The Miecznik programme, whose phases proceed according to schedule, building integrated air defence – Narew, Pilica, Pilica+ programmes, creating an independent production line for 155 mm ammunition – these are just some of our joint initiatives. One of the largest allocations, or our investments in air defence, is being created in cooperation with Great Britain. The selection of submarines by Poland, and deciding on Sweden also happened in cooperation with Great Britain, who will have a large hand in this process. It was one of the most consequential decisions that we have undertaken.
- added the Deputy Prime Minister, noting the most important areas of cooperation.
- We have begun our meeting with the important topic of support for Ukraine. (…) This tyranny, this oppressive, neo-imperial policy of the Russian Federation is a source of harassment for Ukraine since 2014, since the occupation of Crimea and on to the full-scale invasion later. The response of Poland and Great Britain is unambiguous: we will defend liberty with all our might, we will defend our rights and our land, every centimetre of our territory. I believe I can say that during our vis-à-vis meeting the Secretary has proposed a very important message. Among the different international formats, and our ironclad alliances, we have a similar view of the alliance with the United States. Both Poland and Great Britain is in favour of strengthening this transatlantic alliance, and Great Britain is a great example of this – it is from Great Britain that all that is connected to the transatlantic alliance originated. We are in favour of strengthening and building our own capabilities, of greater independence of Europe, but not a disconnect with the United States.
- said the Minister of National Defence.
The signed document maps avenues of strategic cooperation between the Armed Forces of both countries until the end of the decade. The main topics of discussion were matters of adapting the military to hybrid threats, saturating the eastern flank of NATO with modern deterrence potential, as well as strengthening industrial ties. The ministers have also confirmed their unity and coordination in their efforts to support Ukraine.
- This is an important moment in bilateral relations between our countries. The ties of friendship and solidarity between the United Kingdom and Poland go deep, but this is not merely about our shared history – it’s also about our similar assessment of the threats we face today and our joint determination that in this struggle between liberty and tyranny the United Kingdom and Poland will not be passive bystanders. Thanks to the leadership of Poland, its experience and perspective, when Poland calls, the United Kingdom responds. We hear loud and clear what Poland experiences every day, what some call hybrid threats from Russia – I personally prefer to call it state-sponsored terrorism – I see the daily mobilization of your forces and air defence in the face of drone incursions. We are also seeing, not just in Poland but across NATO, how Putin is testing us and tests the determination of NATO. (…) The meaning of what we are doing here today is that it strengthens our capabilities, our defence industry potential and, critically, our alliance. (…) I am thankful for your friendship, support and solidarity. Poland is one of our greatest and, without a doubt, most reliable friends in Europe, and we cherish and nurture this friendship
- noted the British Secretary for Defence Wes Streeting.
>>> GALLERY – The meeting of the defence ministers of Poland and Great Britain

articles.title: US Warns Gulf Countries of Possible New Military Operation Against Iran
articles.body:
The United States has warned several Gulf Arab countries that it could resume military action against Iran after the US midterm elections on November 3.
According to The Wall Street Journal, Washington has reportedly urged regional countries to prepare for a short but intense military campaign against Iran, using diplomatic and military channels to deliver the warning.
According to sources cited by the publication, the United States and Israel are considering a new wave of large-scale strikes against Iran.
The military is already taking preparatory steps. For example, flight-tracking data and information from two officials indicate that an additional Patriot air defense system is being transferred from Texas to Israel to strengthen its defenses against missile attacks.
US forces in the Middle East are replenishing ammunition stocks, while bomber and fighter aircraft prepare for possible strike operations.
In November, another carrier strike group and a Marine Corps unit could join the US force in the region, which currently consists of around 20 warships.
According to the WSJ, the US president has not yet made a final decision on a new military operation but is leaning toward large-scale strikes after the elections. Potential targets include Iran’s infrastructure and nuclear program facilities.
Tehran, in turn, has warned that it could retaliate by striking economic and civilian facilities in countries across the region. Despite previous hostilities, Iran retains a substantial stockpile of missiles and is rebuilding its ballistic weapons production capacity.
Amid the threat of renewed escalation, Iran has begun reinforcing its nuclear infrastructure and preparing its population for possible hostilities.
Militarnyi previously reported that Iran had developed a plan to attack undersea telecommunications cables in the Persian Gulf in the event of a resumption of war with the United States and Israel.
Tehran also plans to obstruct repairs to damaged cables to prolong communications disruptions across countries in the region.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russia’s Largest Steel Plant, Chemical Factory Amid 531 Drone Claims
articles.body:
Ukraine reportedly struck Russia’s largest steel plant and a major chemical factory overnight on Oct. 27-28, with fires reported at both facilities as Russian authorities reported a massive wave of drone attacks across several regions.
On the night of Oct. 27-28, a missile alert was declared in Russia’s Lipetsk Oblast.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The enemy is attempting to attack the industrial infrastructure of Lipetsk. A massive attack is currently being repelled,” the Russian Telegram channel Radar Lipetsk reported.
Later, the channel reported a fire at the Novolipetsk Steel Plant (NLMK). The Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ also confirmed a blaze on the facility’s premises, suggesting that a Russian Pantsir air defense system may have failed to intercept an incoming aerial target.
Igor Artamonov, the governor of the Lipetsk Oblast, later said on Telegram that 45 drones had been shot down over the region overnight.
According to him, drone debris shattered windows in an apartment building in Lipetsk. In one of the region’s gardening cooperatives, a drone fell onto a garden plot next to a house. Another drone fell near a residential building in the Dankovsky District.
“Reports are circulating on social media and messaging apps about a major fire at an industrial facility. This is not true. Drone debris fell in a wooded area, sparking a fire that has now been contained,” Artamonov said.
Zelensky: Europe Must Be Included in November Peace Talks
NLMK is Russia’s largest steel plant and ranks among the 20 largest steel producers in the world. The facility has an annual production capacity of 17 million tons of liquid steel. It was previously targeted in an attack on July.
Chemical plant reportedly targeted in Tula Oblast
Early on the morning of Oct. 28, Tula Oblast Governor Dmitry Milyaev also declared a missile alert. He later reported that the region had come under a massive attack by Ukrainian drones.
“As a result of falling drone debris in Novomoskovsk, damage has been recorded to an apartment building, private homes, and infrastructure in the adjacent industrial zone,” Milyaev wrote.
He added that information about possible casualties and the extent of the damage was still being clarified.
Although Milyaev did not identify the specific industrial facility targeted, he said that laboratories from the Tula Oblast state institution Priroda (Nature) and the regional office of Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s federal consumer rights protection agency, had been dispatched to Novomoskovsk.
According to Exilenova+ and the Russian outlet Astra, the target of the latest attack in Novomoskovsk was the Azot chemical plant, which belongs to the EuroChem group and is one of Russia’s largest producers of nitrogen fertilizers.
The facility manufactures ammonia, ammonium nitrate, urea, and methanol. These substances are used in various industrial applications, including the production of munitions.
Astra previously reported an attack on the Azot chemical plant on June 26. The facility had also caught fire following a Ukrainian attack on the night of June 14.
Moscow claims 531 Ukrainian drones intercepted overnight
The Russian Ministry of Defense reported that air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 531 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) overnight, between 8 p.m. Moscow time on Oct. 27 and 8 a.m. on Oct. 28.
According to the ministry, the drones were intercepted over the Belgorod, Bryansk, Voronezh, Kaluga, Kursk, Lipetsk, Oryol, Rostov, Ryazan, Smolensk, Tambov, and Tula Oblasts, as well as Moscow Oblast.
The Ukrainian side has not commented on its involvement in the reported strikes as of publication.
Previous Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian industrial facilities
On Oct. 24, Ukrainian drones attacked Tolyattikauchuk, a major petrochemical enterprise in Russia’s Samara region.
A fire broke out at the plant, which is owned by Tatneft, and authorities closed nearby streets. The Tolyatti combined heat and power plant (CHP) was also struck, resulting in disruptions to electricity and water supplies for local residents.
Tolyattikauchuk produces monomers, hydrocarbon fractions, and gasoline additives. Its synthetic rubber products are also used in the production of solid rocket fuel for tactical and ballistic missiles.

articles.title: Ukraine, Romania discuss F-16, Patriot, HAWK ammunition supplies, joint drone production
articles.body:
Minister of Defense of Ukraine Yevheniy Khmara, during a phone call with Romania's new Minister of National Defense Ștefan-Radu Oprea, discussed the supply of ammunition for F-16 aircraft and air defense systems, as well as joint drone production under the European SAFE program, the press service of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine reported on Wednesday.
The parties also discussed Russian attacks on ports and vessels in the Black Sea, risks for both countries, and ways to counter them.
Special attention was paid to the supply of ammunition for F-16 aircraft needed for effective counteraction against jet-powered drones, as well as the training of Ukrainian pilots at the F-16 training center in Romania: "This support is important for Ukraine. The greater the number of trained pilots, the larger the fleet of aviation we can deploy and protect the Ukrainian sky. In particular, to shoot down jet drones."
According to him, the sides also discussed Ukraine's need for missiles for Patriot systems required to counter ballistic missiles, as well as ammunition to fight cruise missiles.
"Russia is intensifying its missile attacks; ballistics are one of the main threats. Therefore, we need missiles for Patriot so that our systems can protect people, civilian, and critical infrastructure. In addition, Ukraine needs ammunition to fight cruise missiles. We are talking about missiles for HAWK air defense systems and AIM-9 missiles," the Minister emphasized.
Another area of cooperation was the joint production of drones within the European SAFE program. "Ukraine has technologies and experience that can be useful to our partners, and we are ready to develop mutually beneficial cooperation," Khmara noted.
Khmara congratulated his Romanian counterpart on his appointment and thanked Romania for its aid to Ukraine, particularly for logistical support through its territory.

articles.title: German soldier led local branch of Putin-linked Night Wolves biker club for years, The Insider finds
articles.body:
A Bundeswehr serviceman spent several years leading the German branch of the Night Wolves motorcycle club, and he continues to hold a leadership position with the group. The Insider found a ruling by a German military disciplinary court dismissing the soldier from service. His name was withheld in the ruling, but The Insider identified him as Alexander Sautner, a dual German-Russian citizen. Sautner initially served as vice president of the club’s “Roads of Victory” division, where he was responsible for organizing international motorcycle rallies. In early 2023, Sautner became vice president of the independent German chapter of the biker club: Night Wolves MC Germania. Despite a disciplinary investigation against him, Sautner continued directing the club’s activities and maintaining contacts with its Russian leadership.
A Bundeswehr soldier
The German military court’s ruling describes in detail how a Bundeswehr serviceman came to hold a leadership position in the Night Wolves.
The soldier is not named in the document, but the charges list the actions that formed the basis of the case against him. They include his participation on April 11, 2022, in a Rossiya Segodnya video conference featuring a Soviet flag in the background, several links to RT and Sputnik material that he posted in 2015, and criticism of Polish authorities for refusing to allow a Night Wolves motorcycle convoy to cross their border. According to publicly available information, the only German participant in the aforementioned April 2022 news conference was Alexander Sautner, and the same posts cited in the ruling can be found on Sautner’s Facebook page (1, 2).
According to the court, Sautner was born in Kazakhstan, moved to Russia with his parents at the age of 2, and relocated with his family to Germany in 1994. He holds both Russian and German citizenship.
Sautner joined the Bundeswehr in July 2007 as a noncommissioned officer candidate and attended the German Air Force’s NCO school. After completing his training, he served in transport units, working in vehicle logistics. In February 2010, he was promoted to Stabsunteroffizier, a junior noncommissioned officer rank, and in January 2013 he was transferred to a logistics battalion.
From July to November 2013, Sautner took part in the International Security Assistance Force mission in Mazar-i-Sharif, Afghanistan, receiving the Bundeswehr’s bronze deployment medal for his service. He was also awarded the gold-level military service badge.
A September 2013 performance review described Sautner as an experienced, motivated, and results-oriented noncommissioned officer. His commanders praised his openness, honesty, good relations with fellow soldiers, and overall strong performance. In August 2018, at his own request, Sautner transferred to another unit within the logistics battalion.
Sautner’s Bundeswehr contract was not due to expire until June 30, 2032. However, even before the 2018 transfer, Sautner had begun participating in the activities of the Night Wolves motorcycle club — infamous for its longstanding ties to Vladimir Putin, including its role in Russia’s 2014 annexation of Crimea. According to Germany’s Military Counterintelligence Service, known by its German acronym MAD, Sautner had been a club member since around 2016 and had taken part in its motorcycle rallies even earlier than that.
Sautner later became the first German member of the Night Wolves to achieve “full color” status, meaning full membership in the motorcycle club. In biker culture, “colors” are patches bearing a club’s name and emblem that members wear on their vests. The right to wear the complete set signifies that a person has progressed from supporter and prospective member to a full member of the club.
Sautner later became vice president of the Roads of Victory division, replacing his wife’s uncle in the role. The court ruling does not specify exactly when that happened, but MAD describes him as a longtime vice president and says that until the spring or summer of 2022, he played a key role in organizing and running international motorcycle rallies.
Roads of Victory is a themed Night Wolves division that organizes annual motorcycle rallies around May 9, Russia’s Victory Day commemorating the defeat of Nazi Germany in World War II. Before an independent German chapter was established, Night Wolves activities in Germany were carried out through Roads of Victory, which was headed by Andrei Bobrovsky. Bobrovsky, for his part, is an associate of Night Wolves founder Alexander Zaldostanov, who came under European Union sanctions in 2022. As vice president, Sautner effectively headed Roads of Victory activities in Germany.
The Night Wolves motorcycle club itself was founded by Zaldostanov in 1989. MAD documents say the organization has about 45 chapters in different countries and operates under a strict hierarchy. According to the counterintelligence agency, members are required to follow the club leadership, while Zaldostanov can issue instructions directly to members of foreign chapters.
The Night Wolves and several of the club’s leaders are under EU sanctions for supporting Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. The sanctions justification says the organization spreads Russian propaganda, supports pro-Russian armed formations in Ukraine, and maintains close ties to the Kremlin.
German military counterintelligence regards the Night Wolves’ activities as one instrument of Russia’s hybrid warfare efforts against Germany. MAD assesses that the annual motorcycle rallies are used not only as commemorative events, but also to spread pro-Russian political messages.
How the investigation into Sautner began
The first suspicions among Bundeswehr commanders emerged in 2020, when Sautner’s battalion commander and a security officer noticed a Night Wolves emblem sticker on the rear window of Sautner’s car while it was parked on military premises. At the time, Sautner was working primarily as part of the Bundeswehr’s assistance to civilian health authorities. However, after his links to the Russian motorcycle club were discovered, his commanders concluded that he could no longer be assigned to perform work involving classified information.
Sautner’s former direct superior, whose name was withheld in the ruling, testified that the soldier was primarily assisting civilian health authorities at the time, but the restriction on deploying him to posts requiring security clearance created problems for a unit that had commitments to NATO’s rapid-response forces. The situation was compounded by Sautner’s military specialty, which was in short supply, making him difficult to replace.
Sautner also told the court about the circumstances that prevented him from passing the security vetting required for access to classified information, saying that he had retained Russian citizenship because renouncing it would have involved significant expense. He also refused to sign a pledge not to visit certain countries that were considered potential security risks. The ruling does not identify those countries. Holding a second citizenship is not itself prohibited for Bundeswehr service, and the court documents do not indicate that Sautner concealed the existence of his Russian passport from his commanders.
On Feb. 4, 2021, the Bundeswehr’s logistics command formally opened disciplinary proceedings against Sauter, and in December of that year, he was informed of the main findings, which centered on four Facebook posts he had made between 2015 and 2019. Sautner was offered the opportunity to respond, but declined.
On Jan. 27, 2015, Sauter commented on a Sputnik report about Ukrainian military losses in the Donetsk region, writing that Ukrainians could now try out their crematorium. Military disciplinary prosecutors interpreted the remark as incitement to violence and hatred.
On April 27, 2015, Sautner criticized Polish authorities for refusing to allow Night Wolves participants in a motorcycle rally to transit the country on their way to Berlin. He complained that the bikers were being prevented from honoring those killed in World War II and called the Polish authorities “dirty U.S. vassals.”
On Sept. 4, 2015, Sautner shared an article from the German magazine Compact describing the country as an occupied American colony. He posted another article, this time from RT Deutsch, on June 26, 2019. It concerned historical memory and relations between Russia and the West.
The Insider found the first two posts, which were described in detail in the court ruling, on Sautner’s Facebook page. The court ultimately did not consider the four posts in its final judgment, and they were not brought up during Sautner’s disciplinary hearing because they were unlikely to materially affect the type or severity of the punishment.
Notably, despite the investigation, Sautner continued participating in Night Wolves activities. On May 9, 2021, during one of the Roads of Victory rallies, he was seen carrying the flag of the self-proclaimed “Luhansk People’s Republic.” MAD assessed that displaying the symbol of the unrecognized Russian-backed statelet demonstrated how commemorative events were being used to promote Russian political messages.
Instructions from Night Wolves leaders and a pro-Russian demonstration in Berlin
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, German military counterintelligence uncovered evidence of direct interaction between Sautner and the club’s Russian leadership. MAD materials cited in the court ruling say Sautner maintained direct contact with Alexander Zaldostanov and Andrei Bobrovsky and received instructions from them, including while members of the club leadership were in the war zone in Ukraine.
One such episode occurred in early March 2022, mere days after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion on February 24.
In club correspondence from March 4 and 5, counterintelligence officers found discussions of a demonstration in Berlin that was to be held under the stated aim of opposing alleged persecution of Russian-speaking residents of Germany. According to MAD, Sautner received a personal message containing instructions from Roads of Victory president Bobrovsky, who was referred to as Hauptkommandant, or “commander in chief” in the correspondence. Participants were urged to fight on the “information front.”
Sautner then sent a voice message to the German Roads of Victory group chat strongly urging other club members to attend. On March 5, 2022, Sautner appeared with other Night Wolves members at a demonstration at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate, where he posed with a Russian flag bearing state symbols and the word “Russia.” Photographs from the event were later reviewed by the court.
Sautner said he attended the demonstration to protest discrimination against Russian-speaking people in Germany, adding that he was particularly concerned about his own children. The court, however, viewed the event as a public display of solidarity with Russia staged against the backdrop of the start of its invasion of Ukraine.
The court ruling also mentions another public appearance by Sautner. On April 11, 2022, he participated by video link in a news conference organized by the Russian state media group Rossiya Segodnya. A Soviet flag with a hammer and sickle was visible behind him. MAD interpreted the episode as a further demonstration of Sautner’s senior position within the Night Wolves leadership.
Raising money for Donbas
During the investigation, German military counterintelligence also examined messages from a WhatsApp group called NW DP GERMANY, which was found on Sautner’s phone.
One message asked club members to contribute 1,000 rubles (around $13 at the time) each by Feb. 1, 2022, and then another 500 rubles per month to support Night Wolves chapters in Donbas. The appeal was posted by Denis N., whom German counterintelligence described as a close confidant of Sautner. The person was Denis Nalyotov, who later became head of the club’s German branch.
MAD assessed that the collected funds could have been used to purchase equipment suitable for armed operations against Ukraine. On Feb. 27, 2022, after the full-scale invasion had begun, Sautner himself called on members of the German Roads of Victory organization to send 13 euros each to a person named Badja. According to the message, the money was intended for humanitarian aid to Donbas.
On March 1, Denis Nalyotov discussed the collection with another club member, Thorsten M. He said the money could be sent by PayPal but that it would be better to wait for an in-person meeting and hand it over in cash so the transfers would leave no record.
On April 26, Sautner said in a WhatsApp voice message that around 1,000 euros had been collected. He said the money had been transferred to a fund called “Humanitarian Aid for Donbas.”
MAD materials also cite correspondence from March 2, 2023, in which Badja again called for donations for humanitarian aid. A Roads of Victory representative in Germany replied that fundraising was already underway.
The court ruling does not establish that Sautner personally purchased military equipment or that the funds collected were in fact used for armed activity against Ukraine. The possible military purpose of the money appears specifically as an assessment by MAD.
How Sautner became vice president of Germany’s Night Wolves
In the spring or summer of 2022, Sautner stepped down as vice president of the German Roads of Victory organization, being replaced by Denis Nalyotov. Сounterintelligence assessed that Sautner may have given up the title because of pressure from German law enforcement. Disciplinary proceedings against him were already underway, and MAD documents also refer to an investigation by Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office. The court ruling does not disclose details of that investigation.
The formal transfer of the post, however, did not mean Sautner stopped playing a leadership role. According to MAD, he continued coordinating all major decisions with Nalyotov, with the two generally making and implementing them together.
In early 2023, the Night Wolves established an independent German chapter, Night Wolves MC Germania. Nalyotov became president of the new organization, while Sautner became vice president.
The two informally divided Germany into two zones. Nalyotov ran the northern chapter from Hanover, while Sautner oversaw the south from Bad Mergentheim in Baden-Württemberg. Flight records reviewed by The Insider also indicate that Sautner and Nalyotov traveled to Moscow together after Russia launched its full-scale invasion. (Nalyotov flew from Kaliningrad to Moscow on Jan. 15, 2023, and returned on Jan. 21.)
Sautner therefore obtained a new formal leadership position in the Night Wolves’ German structure after the Bundeswehr’s disciplinary proceedings had already begun. MAD assessed that Sautner’s appointments as club president and vice president indicated a particularly high level of trust from Alexander Zaldostanov. MAD also found that the Russian leadership continued to control foreign chapters, including the organization of propaganda events in Germany.
At the court hearing, Sautner confirmed that he remained a full member of the Night Wolves and continued to serve as vice president of the German chapter.
Why Sautner was not dismissed from the Bundeswehr until 2026
On March 9, 2022, the proceedings were suspended pending additional disciplinary charges. The Bundeswehr’s Federal Office of Personnel Management later considered dismissing Sautner under a law allowing the expedited removal of soldiers involved in anti-constitutional activities without lengthy court proceedings. Sautner was temporarily suspended from official duties in April 2022, and the hearings continued for several more years. On May 26, 2025, the agency determined that there were insufficient grounds execute Sautner’s expedited removal, and the disciplinary case against him continued.
Then on Oct. 10, 2025, Sautner was served with an amended charge sheet. In addition to the earlier Facebook posts, the case now included three new allegations: participation in the pro-Russian demonstration on March 5, 2022; serving as vice president of the German Night Wolves chapter from at least early 2023 through July 29, 2025; and sending an insulting email to a fellow soldier.
The final incident occurred on April 19, 2025. During the night, Sautner emailed a senior NCO in his unit complaining that he had not been informed about the death of a former fellow serviceman. Sautner said the man had died by suicide and accused the command of inaction. The email contained numerous insults directed at members of the unit.
At the court hearing, Sautner apologized to the recipient. The court nevertheless found that he had deliberately violated his duty to treat fellow soldiers with respect.
The court also heard testimony from Sautner’s former commanders, who described him as an experienced, calm, and reliable soldier widely respected by his colleagues. One commander said he had been surprised by the allegations against him.
At the same time, Sautner’s former superiors said that given his actions, they no longer considered his return to the Bundeswehr possible. According to the court ruling, Sautner had openly discussed his Night Wolves activities on his Facebook page, meaning his links to the club were known within his unit.
When Sautner was asked during the hearing whether he even wanted to remain in the Bundeswehr, he was unable to answer immediately. Ultimately, the judges concluded that Sautner had deliberately violated his soldierly duties to remain loyal to Germany, to uphold its constitutional order, and to refrain from conduct that could undermine trust in the Bundeswehr. The court separately stressed that Sautner’s leadership role in an organization closely linked to the Russian state was incompatible with service in Germany’s armed forces.
The ruling also noted that Sautner did not end his Night Wolves activities after the investigation began. On the contrary, while disciplinary proceedings were already underway, he assumed an even more prominent position in the club. The court considered that to be an aggravating factor.
“He can no longer be the servant of two masters,” the ruling said. The judges were quoting wording used by Sautner’s own defense, although the document does not explain the context in which his lawyer used the phrase.
The judges ruled that the Bundeswehr’s trust in Sautner had been irreparably destroyed. On Jan. 28, 2026, Germany’s military disciplinary court found him guilty of disciplinary violations and ordered his dismissal from service. Sautner was also denied special transitional payments following his dismissal and ordered to pay court costs.
The judgment became final on Feb. 5, 2026. The decision was based on Sautner’s leadership role in an organization that German counterintelligence links to the Russian state, his public participation in a pro-Russian demonstration after the start of the full-scale invasion, and his violations of military duties.

articles.title: “Above all, we do not have enough missiles for Patriots”—Zelenskyy after 100+ ballistic missiles
articles.body:
Russia has fired more than 100 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast since 14 October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in his evening address on 27 October. He said partners’ air defense packages are being delayed.
Ukraine’s front-line positions are stronger than they have been in a long time, Zelenskyy said. If partners’ support for Patriots and other air defense remained just as strong, he argued, Ukraine would be in a much better position diplomatically as well. He expects trilateral talks with US and Russian representatives in November. The US, on which, he said, “almost everything concerning Patriots depends,” will be one of the three sides.
Delays and the war on logistics
Overnight on 27 October, Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles and more than 280 drones, in what Zelenskyy called a serious escalation of Russia’s campaign against Ukraine’s logistics. The strikes hit the State University of Trade and Economics campus and the Southern Bridge in Kyiv.
Russian ballistic missiles hit a Kyiv university campus, then return before dawn for the Southern Bridge again
A 46-year-old woman was killed and 15 people were injured, among them dormitory residents and two medics, the Kyiv prosecutor’s office said on the morning of 27 October.
Zelenskyy wrote that artificial and lengthy delays in interceptor packages for Patriots and NASAMS directly help Russia achieve the goals of its terror campaign. In his evening address, he added:
“And everyone hears, everyone sees that right now, it is difficult for us to defend against Russian ballistic missiles. And above all, we do not have enough missiles for Patriots.”
A month waiting on Hegseth
Earlier, on 26 October, Zelenskyy wrote that Ukraine had waited almost a month for US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s signature on missiles for Patriots and NASAMS. Kyiv is also working with Europe and other partners, he added.
Ukraine raises its stalled Patriot request with Washington again after almost a month without Hegseth’s signature
Separately, The Washington Post reported on 19 October that some transfers come from allies and need Hegseth’s approval, because the US must sign off on re-transfers. Zelenskyy’s post does not say whether his wait concerns those transfers.
Before Zelenskyy’s latest statements, US officials rejected claims of a deliberate hold. A US government official called Ukraine’s claims “not true,” the Kyiv Independent reported. On 20 October, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was “nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine.” Hegseth said the US had not changed its posture toward Ukraine but wants “our guys” to have as many interceptors as possible.
