articles.title: Top U.S. general says AI will change how America fights its wars
articles.body:
- Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, called artificial intelligence one of his three strategic priorities, after the budget and ahead of operations.
- Caine used the term super intelligence, which a Sept. 29 executive order directs the executive branch to use in place of artificial intelligence.
Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, has named artificial intelligence as one of his three strategic priorities, ranking it behind only securing a budget and ahead of ongoing military operations.
Caine made the remarks on Oct. 26 during a fireside chat at the National Defense Transportation Association and U.S. Transportation Command fall meeting in Grapevine, Texas, moderated by Transcom commander Gen. Randall Reed of the U.S. Air Force, according to a Pentagon News account of the session. Throughout the discussion, Caine referred to the technology as “super intelligence,” or SI, the term President Donald Trump is trying to substitute for “artificial intelligence” across the federal government.
“I have sort of three strategic priorities right now, separate from [others]. No. 1 is making sure that we have a budget. … No. 2 is [super intelligence], and No. 3 is ongoing operations,” said Caine.
The wording follows a Sept. 29 executive order that directs the executive branch, to the extent the law allows, to use “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in place of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI.” The order does not create a new category of technology. It defines super intelligence as the same systems already covered by the statutory definition of artificial intelligence in federal law, so when Caine says SI, he is describing the AI tools the military uses and develops today.
Trump first announced the change in his Sept. 22 speech to the United Nations General Assembly, saying all U.S. government documents would switch to the “much more accurate term.” The State Department has since ordered its staff to rename AI-related programs and systems, and military offices have started adopting the language as well; the U.S. Marine Corps aviation acquisition office this month described new maintenance tools it is pursuing as predictive super intelligence technologies.
The term already carries a different meaning in the technology field. Researchers and AI companies have long used superintelligence to describe a hypothetical future system that surpasses human intelligence, and the industry more often uses “artificial general intelligence” for AI that would match or exceed people across tasks. Critics have argued that the government’s branding blurs that distinction, and Trump has responded by calling anyone who uses the term “Artificial Intelligence” an enemy of the White House.
Caine told the Transcom audience that the technology will be essential for the joint force to win tactical engagements, run logistics and sustainment, and carry out command and control, the functions that let commanders direct forces in combat. He described a future conflict in which the number of kinetic and non-kinetic actions moving between the United States and an adversary, from missiles, rockets and bombs to cyberattacks, would be significant enough to require machine help.
“When I think of SI, …it’s going to be a game changer as we move forward,” said Caine.
The chairman stressed that the work involves training leaders as well as systems and models, so that future commanders get decision support while humans stay appropriately involved and the military balances the opportunities against the risks. He said the Joint Staff is already working on that effort.
“It’s going to be an important part of our future, [and] we need to lean in,” said Caine.
The Pentagon’s use of the technology has grown quickly over the past year. In May, Under Secretary of War Emil Michael said the number of department personnel using AI tools rose from about 80,000 to 1.5 million in a single year, spanning enterprise productivity software through classified intelligence analysis. The department is also applying AI to missile defense data fusion and has launched a pilot program that uses AI-assisted tools to manage security classification.
Transcom offers an obvious test case for the logistics side of Caine’s argument. The command moves troops, equipment and supplies worldwide by air, sea and land, and the forecasting, routing and maintenance planning behind that work are the kind of data-heavy tasks where the Pentagon has been most willing to put AI tools into daily use. Caine did not describe specific Transcom programs during the session, according to the Pentagon account.
He closed the point by saying the commercial sector is likely to set the pace if past experience holds, and that the military needs to keep up.
“And we need to match them at the same speed and tempo,” Caine said.

articles.title: Chinese expert points to Japan’s ability to produce thousands of nuclear warheads
articles.body:
BEIJING, October 28. /TASS/. Japan possesses more than 40 metric tons of plutonium, theoretically enough to produce several thousand nuclear warheads, Secretary General of the China Arms Control and Disarmament Association (CACDA) Dai Huaicheng told TASS.
He pointed out that according to the Japanese authorities, the country possessed 44.4 tons of separated plutonium at the end of 2024, including 8.6 tons stored domestically and 35.8 tons held overseas. In addition, Japan’s stocks of spent nuclear fuel contain about 191 tons of unseparated plutonium.
"The latest report from the Japan Atomic Energy Commission, published in August 2026, says that the total amount of separated plutonium remained at about 44.4 tons at the end of 2025, with 9.9 tons stored in the country and about 34.5 tons held abroad, as the size of the stocks remained vast," Dai said.
"What does this mean? Making a simple nuclear warhead typically requires only a few kilograms of weapons-grade plutonium. According to open sources, Japan’s 44.4 tons of separated plutonium would be enough to manufacture several thousand nuclear warheads," the expert pointed out.
Dai also said that the Japanese authorities justified the country’s substantial plutonium stockpiles by citing plans to use the material as fuel for nuclear power plants. However, this remains a cause for concern amid statements by some Japanese politicians advocating the acquisition of nuclear weapons, the expert added.
"Although most of Japan’s plutonium is reactor-grade, it’s not entirely impossible to use it in nuclear devices. Notably, Japan has the technology and processing facilities needed to separate weapons-grade plutonium, making the distinction between civilian and military use extremely blurred," the expert concluded.

articles.title: Russia is building drone launch site near Millerovo to launch up to 100 Geran UAVs a day, Ukrainian intelligence says – photos
articles.body:
Russia is building drone launch site near Millerovo to launch up to 100 Geran UAVs a day, Ukrainian intelligence says – photos
Russia is building a new launch site for attack drones near the Millerovo military airfield in Rostov Oblast, which borders temporarily occupied Luhansk Oblast.
Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) on Telegram
Details: DIU said satellite images confirm that the new site is under construction.
Quote: "The configuration of the facility indicates that it is intended for preparing and launching jet-powered attack drones, likely the Geran-4 and Geran-5, as well as their modifications. Early estimates suggest that, once construction is complete, the site will be capable of supporting up to 100 launches per day."
Details: According to DIU, the actual intensity of operations at the site will depend on the supply of ready-made drones, the availability of fuel and warheads, the number of trained crews, the serviceability of equipment, and assigned tasks.
DIU noted that in late August, there were no visible signs of active construction at the site. However, by mid-October, Russian forces had already established launch positions and other infrastructure.
The intelligence agency said the rapid pace of construction could be explained by the use of previously tested technical solutions and by concentrating resources on building relatively simple launch infrastructure.
"The construction of a new drone launch facility just 3.5 km from Millerovo airfield indicates that Russia intends to use the same air defence systems protecting the airfield to defend the new site," DIU added.
It also noted that the new site could benefit from access to the airfield's existing road, communications and logistics infrastructure, as well as its technical support systems.
Russia is also upgrading its jet-powered attack drones. A new version of the Geran-4 has been equipped with additional autonomous navigation capabilities, including an optical terrain-matching system. A similar system is being integrated into the K5 version of the Geran-5 drone.
"In addition, the Russians have equipped the Geran-4 with a domestically produced jet engine and a new warhead designed to strike bridges and electricity transmission towers," DIU said.
The Geran-4 has a range of up to 770 km, while the Geran-5 can fly up to 950 km.
The new facility will expand Russia's network of attack drone launch sites, which, according to DIU, already includes at least 12 permanent facilities. DIU believes the new facility may be part of Russia's preparations to intensify attacks on Ukraine, particularly over the winter.

Background: Ukrainka Pravda previously reported, citing Ukrainian OSINT community Absolutely Reliable Source, that Russia was building the Millerovo drone launch facility. The community said that as of 12 October, the site had eight positions for launchers and 32 areas for preparing drones for launch.

Shoot-down rate of Russian jet-powered drones steadily increasing, General Staff says

articles.title: USA Reinforced the Island of Guam with a New Air and Missile Defense Battalion Equipped with THAAD, Patriot, and UAVs
articles.body:
The U.S. Army has formed and activated a new air and missile defense battalion on the island of Guam in the Pacific Ocean.
The press office of U.S. Army Pacific reported on this.
The ceremony marking the formation of the 3rd Battalion, 43rd Anti-Aircraft Artillery Regiment, 38th Air and Missile Defense Brigade, part of the 94th Air and Missile Defense Command, took place on October 16.
The newly formed unit replaced Task Force Talon, which was deactivated this summer. That task force had been operating on a rotational basis since 2013.
The new battalion will operate THAAD and Patriot anti-aircraft missile systems as well as unmanned aerial vehicles.
THAAD (Terminal High Altitude Area Defense) is a U.S. ground-based missile defense system designed to intercept short-, medium-, and intermediate-range ballistic missiles in the exoatmospheric phase.
The system’s key feature is its ability to destroy aerial targets both in the upper atmosphere and beyond it—at altitudes ranging from 40 to 150 km and at ranges of up to 200 km.
To detect and track ballistic threats out to 1,000 km, the system uses a powerful AN/TPY-2 active phased array radar (APAR).
Guam hosts key U.S. military facilities, including Andersen Air Force Base, which can accommodate strategic bombers, and a naval base that serves as a homeport for nuclear submarines and support ships.
Beyond hosting combat units, the island serves as the main logistics and supply hub for U.S. military operations in the region, with massive fuel storage tanks and ammunition depots.
The U.S. Marine Corps previously formed the first battalion designed to launch medium-range missile strikes.
The upgraded unit’s main weapon is the NMESIS (Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System) missile system.

articles.title: “Our future cannot be the subject of agreements between Trump and Putin”: Ukraine supporters protest US policy on Russia in Europe, US, and Australia
articles.body:
Pro-Ukraine demonstrations took place in more than 10 cities across Europe, North America, and Australia over the past week, with protesters opposing US President Donald Trump’s agreement to resume Russian diesel shipments, the easing of sanctions on Moscow, and restrictions affecting Ukraine’s military support.
The protests were organized by Ukrainian diaspora groups and international supporters of Ukraine, who called on Washington to maintain pressure on the Kremlin, restore Ukraine’s access to Starlink, and stop using military aid and intelligence sharing as leverage against Kyiv.
The International Center for Ukrainian Victory (ICUV) said the actions reflected growing concern over US decisions that could benefit Russia while its war against Ukraine continues.
The demonstrations followed Trump’s announcement on 9 October that Russia would supply diesel to US and global markets. The US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control subsequently issued a temporary license authorizing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel, including imports into the United States, through 7 April 2027.
The decision reversed part of Washington’s restrictions on Russian fuel imposed after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
“We are witnessing a dangerous situation today: Russia, which attacks Ukrainian cities every day, is being offered economic agreements and sanctions relief, while Ukraine is being asked to make concessions. But Ukrainians cannot simply stop fighting. For us, this is a matter of our state’s existence. Our future cannot be the subject of agreements between Trump and Putin. It belongs to Ukrainians,” said Olena Ivashchenko, founder of Campaign for Ukraine.
Protests target Russian fuel deal and pressure on Kyiv
In London, hundreds of protesters gathered outside the US Embassy on 16 October, according to organizers from Campaign for Ukraine and partner groups. Participants included Ukrainians, Britons, Americans, and members of other national communities. British lawmakers also raised the issue in Parliament.
Demonstrators carried signs reading “How Many Ukrainians per Barrel?” and “Occupation Is Not Peace,” calling on Washington to preserve sanctions and reject pressure on Ukraine to make territorial concessions.

Protests also took place in Edinburgh, Chicago, Houston, Boston, San Diego, Prague, Rome, Stockholm, and Sydney. In Prague, two Ukrainian activists staged a protest outside the US Embassy on 21 October, pouring a red liquid resembling blood onto the road to symbolize the human cost of the policy.
Participants in several cities also condemned restrictions on Starlink, delays in ammunition supplies, and disruptions to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
The diesel agreement has drawn criticism in Ukraine because Russian fuel exports generate revenue for Moscow while its forces continue attacking Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. A Russian diesel tanker carrying 40,000 metric tons of fuel departed Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on 22 October bound for New York, according to shipping data reported by Reuters. It was expected to arrive on 7 November.
Organizers warn against easing pressure on Moscow
Protest organizers argued that restoring Russian fuel sales and relaxing sanctions risk helping Moscow finance its war. They also opposed any US effort to secure concessions from Kyiv without requiring Russia to end its aggression.
The demonstrations reflect concerns among Ukraine’s international supporters that Washington’s pursuit of economic agreements with Moscow could undermine efforts to isolate Russia and strengthen Kyiv’s position.
Trump has defended the diesel arrangement as a way to increase fuel supplies and lower prices. His administration has also presented engagement with Moscow as part of its broader effort to end the war, while critics question whether easing economic pressure will produce meaningful concessions from the Kremlin.

articles.title: Nordic call to Putin opens rift in Europe on Ukraine
articles.body:
Nordic call to Putin opens rift in Europe on Ukraine
A phone call with the leaders of Finland and Norway’s with Russian President Vladimir Putin has exposed divisions among Ukraine’s European backers. Denmark criticized the initiative and Sweden complained that it had received no advance notice.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store contacted Putin on Tuesday ahead of renewed Russia-US-Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi next month. The leaders discussed efforts to resolve the conflict, as well as security and stability in Northern Europe and the Baltic Sea.
Most Western European leaders have shunned direct contact with Moscow since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, but now appear to be desperately seeking a seat at the negotiations table. Both Stubb and Store have been named as potential candidates to represent Brussels at the talks, but neither spoke on Europe’s behalf during Tuesday’s call.
Following the conversation, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen accused her Nordic colleagues of breaking ranks, saying she was “very skeptical about this Norwegian-Finnish initiative” because it had “not been coordinated with the rest of us.”
Frederiksen said Europe should stick together rather than go solo, doubting anything can be achieved through unilateral contacts with Moscow.
Her opposition to the diplomatic initiative comes as Copenhagen is backing Kiev’s efforts to expand its weapons production to Danish soil. Ukrainian arms manufacturer Fire Point plans to build a missile-fuel factory in Denmark.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also lamented that he had not been informed of the call to Putin beforehand and said he had “pretty low expectations for this kind of conversation.”
Western leaders have repeatedly faced backlash for contacting Putin or advocating direct talks with Moscow. Earlier this year, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever sparked a wave of backlash from his colleagues after arguing that Europe’s strategy of arming Kiev and sanctioning Russia had failed, leaving negotiations as the only viable option.
His comments elicited an immediate retort by EU Foreign Policy chief Kaja Kallas, who has consistently dragged the bloc down the warpath with Russia. She argued that normalizing ties with Moscow would lead to “more wars.” De Wever’s own foreign minister also described the move as “a signal of weakness.”
In 2024, then-German Chancellor Olaf Scholz was also accused of opening a “Pandora’s box” by calling Putin, with Estonia and other Baltic states decrying contacts with Moscow a “strategic mistake.”
Russian officials have repeatedly accused European governments of prolonging the conflict and obstructing a settlement while demanding a place at the negotiating table. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said in March that the EU had “completely discredited itself” as a mediator, citing its failure to uphold previous agreements and its support for deploying Western troops in Ukraine.
Moscow has nevertheless expressed willingness to engage with a European representative committed to negotiations. On Sunday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said a negotiator from Brussels would be welcome, but stressed that such a person would need to be “someone genuinely committed to facilitating a peaceful settlement.”

articles.title: US costs of Iran war rise to over $47 billion: Pentagon
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US costs of Iran war rise to over $47 billion, according to Pentagon estimate
The US military has spent over $47 billion so far for the war on Iran, more than 25% higher than the Defense Department's estimate in July, according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its estimate, which has not been shared publicly.
The disclosure about the rising cost of the Iran war comes as Republicans wrestle with the political fallout of the unpopular conflict ahead of the 3 November midterm election that will determine control of Congress for the next two years.
The war's impact on global energy costs has weighed on support for Republican candidates and hurt President Donald Trump's approval ratings. Trump's Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress.
The Pentagon's latest estimate was tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than $29 billion to replace expended munitions used in the conflict.
More than $6 billion would be needed to replace military equipment and so-called "platform losses," which include the loss of aircraft including many drones lost during the war.
Trump launched the Iran war jointly with Israel in February, predicting that the conflict would last a short time.
Trump's initial strategy in the Iran war focused on first using expensive, high-end precision missiles to bomb Iran's defenses so it could later use less expensive munitions, including gravity bombs like the air-launched JDAMs, which are plentiful.
But an April ceasefire gave time for Iran to dig out underground storage facilities, bringing back online some Iranian defenses, as well as missiles and drones that had been inaccessible.
Trump has since imposed a naval blockade on Iran to starve it of oil export revenue and held out the possibility of restarting combat operations after the midterm elections. US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, say the Pentagon has been planning to restart heavy fighting if ordered to do so.
The latest Pentagon estimate compares to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's July estimate of $37.5 billion for the cost of the war.
While the figures include a host of operational costs, from flight operations to cyber support, the US military's Iran war cost estimates did not clearly account for the massive expense expected to repair damage to US bases sustained by Iranian missile and drone attacks.

articles.title: Iraq: Drone shot down near US embassy in Baghdad
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iraq: Drone shot down near US embassy in Baghdad
A drone was shot down near the US embassy in Baghdad on Tuesday, triggering three loud explosions near the heavily fortified Green Zone, Iraqi security officials said.
Iraq's Security Media Cell said in a brief statement that the explosions were caused by the interception of a drone near the Green Zone, which houses the US embassy and several government institutions.
Security sources in Baghdad told The New Arab that two surveillance drones had approached the US embassy compound before being intercepted by its C-RAM air defence system.
The sources said Iraqi authorities had launched an investigation but had not yet established where the drones were launched from.
The incident comes as the Iraqi government continues efforts to persuade armed factions to surrender their weapons and bring all military capabilities under state control.
Several factions have agreed to hand over their weapons, but others have refused, including four groups operating under the umbrella of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq.
They are Kataib Hezbollah, Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada, Harakat al-Nujaba and Harakat al-Awfiya.
Security sources told The New Arab that they suspected the drones belonged to factions opposed to disarmament, although no group had claimed responsibility.
The sources said the factions continued to regard the US embassy as an occupation base and possessed surveillance and drone capabilities unmatched by other local Iraqi groups.
Last week, the four factions accused Washington of violating Iraqi sovereignty and failing to honour its commitments to Baghdad.
In a joint statement, they criticised restrictions on airports and border crossings with Iran, arguing that such decisions were being dictated by the United States.
They also questioned whether Iraq could exercise genuine sovereignty while major national decisions remained subject to foreign influence.
Earlier, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi announced that three of five armed factions that had agreed to surrender their weapons had already done so, while negotiations continued with the remaining two.
"Five factions agreed to hand over their weapons, and three have already done so, while dialogue continues with the others," Zaidi said during a meeting with tribal leaders, according to his office.
Iraqi researcher Mujashaa al-Tamimi told The New Arab that the use of surveillance drones could be intended to signal to Washington that armed factions remained active and capable of carrying out operations.
However, he stressed that this interpretation depended on whether the drones had actually been launched by those groups.
Tamimi warned that the renewed use of drones could signal another period of heightened tensions in Baghdad.

articles.title: Iran opposes nuclear technology monopoly, calls for equal access to advanced technologies
articles.body:
Iran opposes nuclear technology monopoly, calls for equal access to advanced technologies
TEHRAN — Iran has called for equitable global access to advanced nuclear technologies, urging the international community to eliminate discriminatory barriers, expand technical cooperation and strengthen protections for peaceful nuclear facilities.
Hossein Derakhshandeh, deputy head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) and chief executive of the Nuclear Power Production and Development Company of Iran, outlined four priorities for the equitable development of nuclear power at the International Ministerial Conference on Nuclear Power in South Korea on Tuesday.
He stressed the need to remove discriminatory restrictions, facilitate access to advanced technologies, broaden technical cooperation and reinforce international measures to protect peaceful nuclear facilities, warning against the use of nuclear technology to establish monopolies.
Derakhshandeh also called for equal access to advanced nuclear technologies in accordance with international law and without double standards. He reaffirmed the inalienable right of states party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) to conduct nuclear research and development and use nuclear energy for peaceful purposes.
Emphasizing the importance of upholding the rights of NPT signatories, he called on the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to function as an independent, technically focused and development-oriented organization, in line with its Statute. The Agency’s mandate includes promoting the peaceful use of nuclear energy and facilitating technical cooperation among member states without discrimination, he said.
However, Derakhshandeh argued that developments in recent years had shown the Agency to be increasingly influenced by political considerations, undermining its impartial implementation of its statutory responsibilities. He cited the US-Israeli attacks on Iran’s peaceful nuclear facilities as an example of the challenges facing the international nuclear framework.
He described the attacks as a flagrant violation of the United Nations Charter, international law, and IAEA General Conference resolutions prohibiting attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities. He also criticized the Agency for an 'inadequate response,' saying it had failed to uphold the fundamental principles of impartiality and professionalism effectively.
Derakhshandeh stressed that protecting peaceful nuclear infrastructure was a shared international responsibility. He also condemned 'international silence over violations of the Iranian people’s rights' in areas including energy, healthcare, food security, the environment and industry.
He further criticized the Israeli regime, the United States and certain European countries for 'politically motivated campaigns' against Iran, involving unfounded accusations and negative media coverage.
His remarks underscored Iran’s call for a nuclear order grounded in equal access to technology, respect for the peaceful-use rights of NPT signatories. and the consistent application of international law, free from political pressure and discriminatory treatment.

articles.title: Germany’s Special Operations Forces Are Reorienting for War with Russia
articles.body:
The Bundeswehr’s Special Operations Forces Command (KSK) is reorienting its training toward a potential war with Russia and preparing its units for prolonged operations on NATO’s eastern flank.
KSK Commander Brigadier General Andreas Kühne told the German newspaper BILD about this.
According to him, typical special forces operations were previously planned to last about three days, after which the unit would return to base to rest and replenish supplies.
In the event of a war with Russia, the command assesses that this format would be unsuitable.
“We are very specifically focused on the enemy—Russia,” Kühne stated.
He noted that units will have to remain in the field for much longer periods without the ability to quickly return to a secure base.
“Perhaps initially with no end date at all,” the KSK commander noted.
In this regard, special forces are practicing operations against an adversary equipped with armored vehicles, artillery, drones, and electronic warfare systems.
Special attention is being paid to operating in the low temperatures characteristic of a potential theater of operations on NATO’s eastern flank.
According to Kühne, if a real threat emerges, KSK units must begin carrying out their missions before the main ground forces are deployed.
He cited the Bundeswehr’s 45th Tank Brigade, deployed in Lithuania, as an example.
“When the 45th Tank Brigade in Lithuania actually starts its engines in a real-world scenario, we want our work to already be done,” the KSK commander explained.
According to him, upon receiving an order, the unit can depart Stuttgart by air within four hours, carrying the necessary equipment to carry out the mission.
This includes, in particular, reconnaissance deep within enemy territory, special operations, and other tasks designed to create conditions for the main forces to operate.
Küne also said the Russian military leadership must know the capabilities of German special forces.
During exercises in the Baltic states, Germany has already demonstrated its special forces’ capabilities.
The KSK commander called this a kind of “price” for potential aggression, intended to make an attack on NATO countries too costly for Russia.
The KSK’s reorientation comes amid broader changes in the Bundeswehr’s preparations to defend Germany and NATO’s eastern flank.
The German military regularly conducts exercises involving force deployment, the protection of critical infrastructure, the defense of allied nations, and operations against a technologically advanced adversary.
Heimatschutz reservists also participate in these scenarios; in the event of war, they are tasked with protecting key military and civilian facilities, troop movement routes, logistics hubs, and rear-area infrastructure.
Special attention is paid to making training conditions as close as possible to those of an actual battlefield.
During the Taurus 2024 series of exercises, specialized paratroopers from the 2nd Company of Fallschirmjägerregiment 31 practiced trench warfare, countering armored vehicles, airborne assault operations, and searching for enemy forces in their own rear.
One element of the exercises involved engaging a real, demilitarized Soviet-designed BMP-1 used as a moving armored target.
According to the scenario, a reconnaissance drone first detected the vehicle, after which groups of paratroopers advanced to positions to engage the armored vehicle with anti-tank weapons.
To ensure the vehicle’s safe reuse during training, an additional steel plate was installed on its rear.
During other phases of Taurus 2024, paratroopers were deployed by NH90 and CH-53 helicopters; they practiced urban combat and operations against an enemy that had penetrated the rear and could attack bridges, warehouses, airfields, and railway junctions.
Such exercises demonstrate the Bundeswehr’s shift from scenarios involving short-term expeditionary operations to preparing for a protracted, high-intensity conflict in Europe.
Currently, approximately 1,500 military personnel and civilian employees serve in the Kommando Spezialkräfte (KSK).
Of these, about one-third belong directly to the special operations units, while the rest provide command, logistics, and other functions.
According to Kühne, the KSK’s staffing level is approximately 70–80%.
The selection process remains rigorous—only slightly more than 15% of candidates successfully pass it.
The command expects that an increase in the Bundeswehr’s overall strength will allow for an expanded pool of candidates for selection into the special forces unit.
Training at the KSK center in Calvi includes marksmanship drills, close-quarters combat, physical training, swimming, martial arts, and operations in harsh climatic conditions.
According to BILD, the units use up to 500,000 rounds of ammunition during the course of a year of training.
The KSK was established in 1996 to carry out the most complex special operations, including hostage rescues, countering terrorist groups, evacuating people from crisis regions, and conducting reconnaissance behind enemy lines.
In particular, the unit has carried out combat missions in Afghanistan against the Taliban.

articles.title: SBU detains pair of Russian militants who fled front, tried to reach Kyiv disguised as civilians
articles.body:
Counterintelligence of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) has detained two contract soldiers of the 291st Motorized Rifle Regiment of the Southern Military District of Russia in the frontline area of Donetsk region who, posing as civilians, were hitchhiking toward Kyiv, the SBU reported.
"SBU employees detained them at a checkpoint at the entrance to Dnipropetrovsk region. A military ID tag of the Russian army was found around the neck of one of the perpetrators," the SBU said in a statement on its Telegram channel on Wednesday.
According to the Ukrainian special service, the occupiers hoped to reach Kyiv—where relatives of one of the militants live—and "lay low."
As the investigation established, one of the detainees turned out to be a resident of temporarily occupied Dovzhansk in Luhansk region, twice convicted of murder, who has been fighting on the side of the enemy against the Defense Forces since 2016.
"After the start of the full-scale war, the recidivist took part in battles near Bakhmut as an assistant gunner of an anti-tank missile system," the agency specified.
Another perpetrator, according to the SBU, is a citizen of Russia who signed a contract with the Ministry of Defense of the aggressor state while serving a prison sentence for murder.
The Ukrainian special service specified that both militants were recently sent to storm the positions of Ukrainian troops in the Kramatorsk direction, where they subsequently fled the line of contact and entered a village in the "gray zone."
"There, they changed into civilian clothes found in an abandoned house, buried their uniforms and service weapons of the Russian army in that house, and set off on foot toward the district center. On the way to the city, they stopped a car whose owner agreed to give them a ride to Dnipro, from where they planned to reach Kyiv," the report states.
Security Service investigators notified the enemy accomplice from Luhansk region of suspicion under two articles of the Criminal Code of Ukraine: Parts 1, 2 of Article 111 (high treason committed under martial law) and Part 7 of Article 111-1 (collaborative activity).
An investigation is ongoing to establish all the circumstances of the crime. The perpetrator is in custody without the right to bail.
"His accomplice—a citizen of Russia—is currently being held as a prisoner of war," the SBU noted.
The comprehensive measures were conducted by employees of the Main Directorate of the SBU in Donetsk and Luhansk regions under the procedural guidance of Donetsk Regional Prosecutor's Office.

articles.title: Russia test-fires Bulava from one of its newest missile submarines
articles.body:
- Russia’s Generalissimo Suvorov submarine fired a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile from the Sea of Okhotsk on Oct. 28, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
- The missile was launched from underwater toward the Chizha test range in the Arkhangelsk region, and the Pacific Fleet said its warheads arrived on schedule.
The Russian Pacific Fleet’s ballistic missile submarine Generalissimo Suvorov fired a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile from beneath the Sea of Okhotsk on Oct. 28, sending it across the country to the Chizha test range in the Arkhangelsk region, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
The ministry said the launch was carried out from a submerged position as part of the crew’s planned combat training, and the Pacific Fleet said that, according to tracking data, the missile’s warheads arrived in the designated area at the planned time. The flight path took the missile from Russia’s Far East to the far north of its European territory, a route the Pacific Fleet uses to test the readiness of its strategic submarines.
“The crew of the Project 955A Borei-A class strategic nuclear-powered missile submarine Generalissimo Suvorov of the Pacific Fleet, in accordance with the combat training plan, test-fired a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile aimed at the Chizha test range in the Arkhangelsk region,” the Russian Defense Ministry said.
The K-553 Generalissimo Suvorov is one of Russia’s newest strategic submarines and the third of the upgraded Borei-A class, a fourth-generation design from the Rubin Central Design Bureau in St. Petersburg. The Sevmash shipyard in Severodvinsk laid it down on Dec. 26, 2014, and the Russian Navy commissioned it on Dec. 29, 2022. Before entering service, the submarine fired a Bulava from the White Sea on Nov. 3, 2022, with the warheads striking the Kura test range on the Kamchatka Peninsula, the opposite direction to this week’s flight.
In 2023, the submarine sailed from the Northern Fleet to the Pacific along the Northern Sea Route and arrived at its permanent base in Vilyuchinsk on Kamchatka on Oct. 16, 2023, where it joined the 25th submarine division. TASS reported that the boat’s imported components have been replaced with Russian-made equipment.
Each Borei-class submarine carries 16 Bulava missiles. The Bulava is a solid-fuel missile developed by the Moscow Institute of Thermal Engineering, the design bureau behind the Topol-M and Yars land-based missiles, and it is launched from underwater so the submarine does not have to surface and reveal its position. Each missile can carry multiple nuclear warheads that separate and fly to individual targets, and the Barents Observer has reported that each Bulava carries six. Russia formally accepted the missile into service in May 2024 after years of testing that began with a first launch in 2005.
The Sea of Okhotsk-to-Chizha route has been used before by Pacific Fleet submarines. In December 2020, the Borei-class Vladimir Monomakh fired a salvo of four Bulava missiles from the same sea toward the same range in the Arkhangelsk region, the first time a Borei had launched four missiles in a single salvo.
Russia’s Borei and Borei-A submarines are replacing the Soviet-era Delta-class boats that carried the naval leg of Russia’s nuclear deterrent for decades, with the Generalissimo Suvorov and its sister ships forming the core of the Pacific Fleet’s strategic submarine force at Kamchatka.

articles.title: Air defenses neutralize 71 Russian drones overnight
articles.body:
Air defenses neutralize 71 Russian drones overnight
The Ukrainian Air Force said this in a Telegram post, Ukrinform reports.
According to the military, starting at 18:00 on Tuesday, October 27, Russia attacked Ukraine with an Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missile launched from Taganrog and 88 attack UAVs, including Shahed-type drones (38 of them jet-powered), S8000 Banderol/Dan-T missiles, Gerberas, and Parodiya-type decoy drones. The attacks came from the directions of Oryol and Kursk in Russia and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
Preliminary data indicate that, as of 08:00 on Wednesday, October 28, air defenses had shot down or suppressed 71 drones.
Several attack UAVs remain in the air, with combat operations ongoing.
Impacts were recorded at eight locations, while debris from downed targets fell at two locations.

articles.title: Ukraine intercepts nearly 60% of Russia’s Geran-4 jet drones, General Staff says, as Kyiv races to counter evolving threat
articles.body:
Ukraine’s air defenses have been intercepting nearly 60% of Russian Geran-4 jet-powered attack drones over the past three months, with the interception rate reaching 80% during some attacks, Ukraine’s General Staff said.
Russia has increasingly used jet-powered drones in its attacks on Ukraine, adding a faster-moving threat to the Shahed-type drones Moscow deploys against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. Ukraine is working to improve interception rates while reducing the cost of countering these aerial threats amid shortages of surface-to-air missiles.
The General Staff’s update did not mention interception rates for Russia’s more advanced Geran-5 jet-powered drone.
F-16s, Mirage jets help intercept Russian drones
According to the General Staff, tactical aviation plays a significant role in destroying Russian jet-powered drones. Ukraine uses F-16s, French Mirage aircraft, and MiG-29 fighters to intercept them.
The military is also strengthening what it calls “short-range air defense” as Ukraine faces a shortage of guided anti-aircraft missiles. These systems include Gepard and Shilka anti-aircraft guns, newer Skynex, Skyranger, and Terrahawk Paladin systems, interceptor drones, and mobile fire groups deployed by different branches of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
Mobile fire groups are equipped not only with machine guns and supporting equipment but also with man-portable air-defense systems (MANPADS). Ukrainian troops have been successfully using these missiles to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones, the General Staff said.
Denmark rushes 50,000 cannon rounds to Ukraine to help F-16s hunt Russia’s advanced jet drones
Ukraine tests cheaper drone interceptors
Ukraine is also seeking to lower the cost of countering Russian aerial attacks by testing new interceptor drones.
According to the General Staff, some models have already downed dozens of Russian Geran jet-powered drones. The military did not provide further details about the interceptor models or the number of drones destroyed.
The rising interception rate reflects Ukraine’s efforts to adapt its air defenses to Russia’s evolving drone campaign while preserving scarce and expensive air-defense missiles for threats that require them.

articles.title: Licensed, not banned: what China’s new rules mean for the parts inside Russia’s Shahed-type drones
articles.body:
China’s updated drone export rules will cover the engines in Russia’s Geran attack drones, Russia’s version of Iran’s Shahed, Ukraine’s sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said on 27 October. He cited a clarification from China’s Commerce Ministry, Ukrainska Pravda’s defense desk Oboronka reported. The license requirement takes effect on 18 November.
Licensing itself isn’t new. China has required permits for some drone engines since September 2023. Even so, Chinese engines kept reaching Russian drone plants, some shipped as refrigeration units, Reuters reported. Russia’s jet-powered Gerans rely fully on Chinese turbojets, HUR deputy chief Vadym Skibitskyi has said. So the update’s value lies in enforcement, not in the list.
Three agencies, one list
Beijing issued the update in a joint announcement by the Commerce Ministry, the General Administration of Customs, and the Central Military Commission’s Equipment Development Department. Announcement No. 49 bars exports of listed drone items without a license, including specially designed autopilots and certain drone engines. China will approve applications that comply with the rules, a Commerce Ministry spokesperson added.
Vlasiuk said the core of Russia’s long-range strike drones has formally come under control. He named engines for Gerans, turbojets for their jet versions, autopilots, and jam-resistant navigation. The announcement lists anti-jam navigation as a technology, not as hardware. He called the step an opening for Ukraine because Beijing now formally takes responsibility for these categories. Kyiv will press for the rules to be applied to known suppliers of Russia’s arms industry and, with partners, track licenses, transit routes, and re-exports, he said.
Permits, refusals, and FPV parts
Licensing does not mean a ban, Vlasiuk stressed. Exporters China deems reliable can get general permits for up to three years, while the rules leave broad grounds for refusal. The new thresholds do not cover motors and speed controllers for FPV drones, batteries, cameras, or optical fiber, he added.
The rules do cover brushless motors that meet all of these: at least 48 volts, at least 3 kW, a power density of at least 3 kW per kilogram, and no more than 3,000 rpm. Their speed controllers are covered too, Militarnyi reported. Russia could still obtain parts with Beijing’s approval, the outlet noted. Ukraine, without such close ties, could face delays, inspections, and higher costs.

articles.title: Finnish and Norwegian leaders discuss Ukraine peace with Putin as a source close to the Kremlin warns of escalating hybrid warfare with Europe
articles.body:
Finnish and Norwegian leaders discuss Ukraine peace with Putin as a source close to the Kremlin warns of escalating hybrid warfare with Europe
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre spoke by phone with Vladimir Putin. Western leaders initiated the call to discuss Russia’s war against Ukraine and diplomatic efforts to end it.
The Finnish president’s office said the call was meant “to convey messages directly regarding future negotiations to help to end the war to President Putin” ahead of meetings to be held in Abu Dhabi. It was Putin’s first contact with European leaders supporting Ukraine since July 2025, when he spoke with French President Emmanuel Macron.
The Kremlin confirmed the call, saying Putin “assessed the current situation” in Ukraine and reminded participants of the “root causes of the conflict.” Putin also pointed to the “confrontational policy of EU and NATO countries, which is prolonging the fighting,” the Kremlin’s press service said.
Volodymyr Zelensky said Stubb and Støre briefed him on their call with Putin. “Alex and Jonas made it clear to the Russian leader that real de-escalatory steps are needed regarding our energy and infrastructure,” Zelensky said. He added that the Finnish and Norwegian leaders had discussed preparations for a trilateral meeting between negotiating teams from Ukraine, the United States, and Russia.
Stubb’s office said the call “was a follow-up of the meeting in Oslo on October 20 and held in consultation with Ukraine.” The Norwegian capital hosted talks that day between Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and Zelensky, with Støre and Stubb also taking part. Witkoff then traveled to St. Petersburg to meet with Putin before returning to Oslo and flying home to the United States.
Those trips produced an agreement on a trilateral meeting between the United States, Ukraine, and Russia, to be held in Abu Dhabi. The meeting will take place after November 4, Putin aide Yuri Ushakov said. The day before, on November 3, the United States will hold midterm elections in which Republicans could lose their congressional majority.
Announcing the timing, Ushakov said the peace talks would also have to involve “all of Europe.” Europe has long sought a negotiator to represent the European Union’s interests in talks on ending the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Stubb has repeatedly been named as a candidate for the role, having built a good relationship with Trump, including on the golf course, and emerged as one of Trump’s main points of contact with European leaders. The Telegraph has also named Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, and Czech President Petr Pavel among the candidates.
After Stubb and Støre’s call with Putin, Frederiksen criticized the initiative, saying she was “skeptical” and that the talks had not been coordinated with other European leaders. She added that she sees no sign that Russia wants peace with Europe, either in the hybrid war that continues every day or in Ukraine.
The independent Russian political newsletter Faridaily says contacts between European leaders and the Kremlin amount to “a significant shift in position.” European leaders had “mostly preferred not to talk to Putin at all” since the war began.
However, a source close to the Kremlin said that “events are moving toward escalation, including an intensification of hybrid warfare with Europe.” According to the source, Putin is convinced NATO is waging a hybrid war against Russia and blames Ukraine’s European allies for “comprehensive assistance” in attacks on Russia, including helping identify targets and guide strikes.
A source close to the Kremlin told Reuters that Putin told Stubb and Støre that Russia would not abandon its goal of capturing all of the Donbas. The European leaders responded that a “just” peace was necessary, the source added.

articles.title: NATO spots Russian submarine in the High North
articles.body:
A Russian Kilo class submarine has been observed in the High North by Standing NATO Maritime Group 1, according to NATO Maritime Command.
The command said: “SPOTTED: A Russian Kilo-class submarine in the High North, observed by Standing NATO Maritime Group 1 (SNMG1).
“Anti-submarine warfare is a team effort. Ships, submarines, aircraft and helicopters from across the Alliance work together every day to detect, track and, if necessary, counter any threat beneath the surface. Our posture is defensive, our readiness is credible, and our resolve is clear: to deter aggression and keep our one billion people across Europe and North America safe.”
Standing NATO Maritime Group 1 is one of the alliance’s permanently available naval forces, drawing warships from member navies on rotation and operating principally in the North Atlantic and northern European waters. The Royal Navy contributes to it regularly and has commanded it in the past.
The Kilo class is a diesel-electric attack submarine built in large numbers from the 1980s, and the improved Project 636.3 boats are quiet enough on batteries to have earned the nickname Black Hole from American analysts. Russia operates them in the Northern Fleet, the Baltic, the Black Sea and the Pacific, and the type carries torpedoes, mines and the Kalibr land attack cruise missile.
The Defence Committee reported this month that Britain does not have what it needs in the High North, urging ministers to retain Type 23 frigates until the Type 26 arrives and questioning whether the Royal Navy’s attack submarines are putting to sea as often as they should. The committee also called for the return of under-ice submarine skills and warned that Britain sells its nuclear contribution to NATO short.
HMS Prince of Wales is currently in the Arctic and North Atlantic on the second phase of Operation Firecrest with the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless, carrying Merlin Mk2 anti-submarine helicopters among her air group, and RAF Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft operate over the northern approaches from Lossiemouth. NATO warships began the current High North deployment earlier in the year.

articles.title: Elon Musk argues that the threat of Russian anti-satellite attacks is a reason to restrict Starlink’s military use in Ukraine
articles.body:
Elon Musk argues that the threat of Russian anti-satellite attacks is a reason to restrict Starlink’s military use in Ukraine
Starlink service for Ukraine’s armed forces was restricted over fears that Russia would shoot down the company’s satellites, a post on X by SpaceX chief Elon Musk suggests. Musk was responding to a post about Russia’s ability to blow up satellites in space.
“This is indeed one of the main reasons that Starlink must remain a civilian operation,” Musk tweeted. “It can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back. An adversary blowing up Starlink satellites would create a domino effect of destruction that would generate a vast field of debris making space unusable.”
In mid-October, Ukraine’s armed forces encountered restrictions on their Starlink satellite terminals, specifically the military version, Starshield. Connections cut out when drones flew faster than 160 kilometers per hour (about 100 mph).
Western media reported that Musk himself had initiated the restrictions on Starlink service for the Ukrainian military. He later accused Ukraine of using Starlink for “offensive” drone strikes. Ukraine’s armed forces responded that this was “technically impossible,” since Starlink does not work over Russian territory.

articles.title: Trump says meeting with Putin, Zelenskyy to be arranged 'very soon'
articles.body:
Ahmet Salih Alacaci
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
US President Donald Trump said early Wednesday that a meeting involving Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy would be arranged "very soon," while also declining to rule out additional US strikes on Iran after next week's US midterm elections.
Speaking to reporters after returning from campaign rallies in Texas, Trump said he had discussed both conflicts with Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Special Envoy Steve Witkoff aboard Air Force One.
"I think with Russia we're making a lot of progress with Russia-Ukraine. There'll be a meeting set up very soon," he said.
Asked who would attend, Trump replied, "President Putin and President Zelenskyy," without providing any further details on the meeting's timing, location, or format.
Moscow and Kyiv last held US-mediated peace negotiations earlier this year, with three rounds of talks this January and February, in Abu Dhabi and Geneva. A meeting between the two countries’ presidents would be unprecedented since the start of the war in 2022.
Turning to Iran, Trump claimed Tehran wanted to reach an agreement with the US but was delaying negotiations, possibly until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
"I think with Iran, we're in a very good position. It's a question of, when do I want to end it?" he said, reiterating his recent views on the conflict.
Asked whether he planned additional strikes against Iran after the elections, Trump declined to give a definitive answer.
"Anything's possible, but I can't tell you,” he said.
The war between Washington and Tehran began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, triggering a wider regional conflict that remains unresolved despite a ceasefire and an agreement to finalize a peace deal.

articles.body:

Poland and the United Kingdom have signed the Warsaw Defence Plan, an agreement to enhance their cooperation on security. The aim, says the British Ministry of Defence, is to “deter Russian threats”.
The plan, which follows on from the two countries signing a strategic defence partnership earlier this year, will include joint development and production of defence technologies and military exercises in the Baltic Sea.
The UK and Poland share a deep and historical defence partnership.
Today, Defence Secretary @WesStreeting signed the Warsaw Defence Plan to bring our two nations’ Armed Forces and industries closer together and help ensure collective security in Europe. 🇬🇧🤝🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/IP98D1Qs1L
— Ministry of Defence 🇬🇧 (@DefenceHQ) October 27, 2026
“Poland is one of the UK’s closest allies – from flying together in the Battle of Britain, to breaking the Enigma code, they have been a vital partner for our defence for nearly a century,” said British defence secretary Wes Streeting on a visit to Warsaw.
“The new Warsaw Defence Plan honours this cooperation and sets out how we will continue to work together today, building a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO,” he added.
His Polish counterpart, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, declared that “the Polish-British alliance has never been as strong as it is now”. Both he and Streeting also emphasised the importance of working together to support Ukraine.
Among the aims listed for the plan are collaboration in the development and manufacture of next-generation air-defence missiles, as well as drones and counter-drone technologies.
Earlier this year, Poland and the UK, along with Germany, France and Italy, agreed to jointly develop and procure air-defence systems, including missiles and drones.
The Warsaw Defence Plan also pledges to “increase defensive maritime activity in the Baltic Sea through exercises and regional coordination, helping British and Polish forces protect vital lines of communication in the sea”.
The two countries will also seek to build upon existing cooperation between their defence industries, including Poland’s purchase of CAMM-ER surface-to-air missiles and 100 launchers from MBDA and last year’s strategic partnership on ammunition production between Poland’s PGZ and Britain’s BAE Systems.
Poland and the UK have signed a major new defence and security treaty.
The agreement includes plans to jointly develop a new air-defence missile, hold large-scale military exercises, and cooperate on countering Russian hybrid attacks https://t.co/cXeYT2u1lw
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 27, 2026
This week’s agreement builds upon the Northolt Treaty signed by Poland and the UK in May this year, under which the two countries agreed to cooperate more closely on security.
Last year, Poland signed a similar agreement upgrading relations with France. That followed a strategic partnership agreement with Sweden the previous year.
In April this year, Poland signed new comprehensive strategic partnership agreements with South Korea and Japan. This year, it has also deepened security ties with Canada and Norway.
In November, Poland will host the first military exercises organised by the so-called Coalition of the Willing. Thousands of personnel from the UK, Poland, France and Germany will test operational readiness for a multinational force to secure a potential future Ukraine peace deal.

articles.title: Ukrainian monitors report fire near Russian plant that sold steel to an S-400 missile builder
articles.body:
A fire broke out in the area of a major Russian steel plant in Lipetsk late on 27 October, Kyiv time, as air defenses fired at incoming targets, the Ukrainian monitoring Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported. Ukrainian partisans said the strike may have hit the plant. The region’s governor denied any large industrial fire.
Whether or not it was hit, the plant matters to Ukraine. The Novolipetsk Metallurgical Plant (NLMK) is Russia’s only producer of electrical steel, Ukrainska Pravda reported in April 2025. NLMK’s tax records, obtained by the outlet, showed sales of that steel to Moscow’s Avangard plant, which builds missiles for S-400 air defense systems. Russia also fires those missiles at ground targets in Ukraine.
Pantsir fires, no visible hit
The targets over Lipetsk were jet-powered, Exilenova+ wrote, citing preliminary reports of impacts and a fire toward the city’s airfield. Footage it posted showed a Pantsir air defense system firing, and the channel suggested the system may have failed to cope. It then reported the fire near NLMK, blaming air defense fire or a falling object.
The Crimean Tatar-Ukrainian partisan movement Atesh said its agents in Lipetsk reported an impact, and in a follow-up said they believe it may have hit NLMK.
Contracts and denials
A 2022 investigation by Disclose and its partners tied 18 NLMK contracts, all signed after 2014, to eight Russian defense firms, including an S-300 maker. NLMK confirmed the contracts but said only a “negligible” amount of civilian steel grades went to those firms.
On 28 October, Lipetsk Oblast Governor Igor Artamonov claimed air defenses downed 45 drones over the oblast overnight. He insisted reports of a large industrial fire were untrue, saying drone debris fell in a tree belt and sparked a fire, since contained. Debris also blew out windows in a Lipetsk apartment block, and one person sought medical help but needed no hospitalization, he added. Whether NLMK took any damage remains unconfirmed.
Earlier strikes on weapons suppliers
Earlier, UK-supplied Storm Shadow missiles reportedly struck a battery plant in Yelets, in the same oblast, on 25 October. Two days before that, they reportedly hit an electronics plant in Oryol. OSINT channels described both as suppliers of parts for Russian missiles.

articles.title: UN chief appoints Russian diplomat to oversee mine action and police
articles.body:
UN chief appoints Russian diplomat to oversee mine action and police
UN Secretary-General António Guterres has announced the appointment of Russian ambassador Gleb Desyatnikov as Assistant Secretary-General for Mine Action and Police in the Department of Peace Operations.
Source: the UN Secretary-General's office
Details: Desyatnikov will lead the division responsible for coordinating the UN's mine action activities and police contingents serving in peacekeeping missions around the world.
The organisation said the diplomat has "more than 35 years of experience in international relations, political affairs and security issues across government, multilateral diplomacy and conflict-affected regions".
He has served as Russia's ambassador to Jordan since 2018. Before that, from 2010 to 2018, he was deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa Department of Russia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Earlier, he worked as a senior adviser on Middle East and North Africa affairs at the Permanent Mission of the Russian Federation to the United Nations in New York from 2004 to 2010. Between 1994 and 1997, he was seconded to the UN Special Commission on Iraq (UNSCOM). Desyatnikov graduated from the Moscow State Institute of International Relations and speaks English and Arabic.
Background:
- In April 2017, António Guterres appointed another Russian representative, Alexandre Zouev, as Assistant Secretary-General for Rule of Law and Security Institutions (OROLSI) in the UN Department of Peacekeeping Operations. Zuev's portfolio included key areas such as the UN peacekeeping police, justice reform, prison systems and the UN Mine Action Service (UNMAS).
- In March 2022, the UN General Assembly voted overwhelmingly to condemn Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and called for the immediate withdrawal of Russian troops. At the time, Ukrainian diplomats urged the UN Secretariat to remove Russian citizens from senior and sensitive security-related positions.
- In March 2023, the International Criminal Court in The Hague issued an arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin over the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children. That same month, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry posted a report documenting evidence of widespread torture, executions of civilians and sexual violence committed by Russian forces in Ukraine.
- In addition, Russian military structures and private military companies have repeatedly contributed to the closure of UN peacekeeping missions in Africa, including in Mali and the Central African Republic, where they support military juntas and have been named in human rights reports concerning mass killings of civilians.
- In April 2024, UN bodies and the Ukrainian government stated that Ukraine had become the most heavily mined country in the world. As a result of the actions of the Russian military, more than 156,000 sq km of Ukrainian territory require surveying and clearance of mines and unexploded ordnance.

articles.title: Nuclear ambitions threaten Japan’s future, Chinese expert warns
articles.body:
BEIJING, October 28. /TASS/. The nuclear ambitions of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s current cabinet could put the future of more than 100 million Japanese citizens at risk, despite widespread public opposition to nuclear weapons, Secretary General of the China Arms Control and Disarmament Association (CACDA) Dai Huaicheng told TASS.
He noted that statements by some Japanese politicians calling for the country to acquire nuclear weapons ran counter to Tokyo’s commitments to peace, as well as the views of the Japanese public.
"Opinion polls conducted by Japanese media show that 60% of the population opposes the development of nuclear weapons, while 80% demand respect for the three non-nuclear principles. This clearly demonstrates the anti-nuclear stance of the majority of Japanese society. Open attempts by Japanese ruling circles to promote the ‘nuclear option’ are putting the future of more than 100 million Japanese people at risk," Dai stressed.
"No one should forget history or go against the will of the people. If Japan’s ruling circles persist in their nuclear delusions and continue to compound their mistakes, this will not only pose a major challenge to the post-war world order and the international system of nuclear non-proliferation, but also run counter to Japan’s peace commitments and the general opinion of the Japanese people, ultimately exacting an extremely high price," he added.
"The international community must call on Japan to deeply reflect on the history of [its] aggression [during World War II], completely break with militarism, finally abandon ambitions to acquire nuclear weapons, and faithfully fulfill its international non-proliferation commitments," the expert concluded.
Non-nuclear principles
Japan maintains three non-nuclear principles: not possessing, not producing and not permitting the introduction of nuclear weapons into its territory. Although the principles aren’t enshrined in laws, all Japanese prime ministers have so far reaffirmed commitment to them. Discussions of the issue have long been considered taboo, prompting some politicians to refer to the "fourth principle" of not discussing nuclear weapons and call for abandoning at least this unwritten rule.
After Sanae Takaichi took office as prime minister, the Japanese media reported that the approach to the three non-nuclear principles would be discussed as part of a planned review of the country’s national security strategy. Media outlets claimed that Takaichi was prepared to call for lifting at least the ban on bringing US nuclear weapons to Japan. However, the prime minister said she had not instructed officials to review the non-nuclear principles as part of discussions of a new version of the national security strategy.

articles.title: The Mecca Pact courts Iran: Containment comes full circle
articles.body:
For nearly half a century, Iran’s adversaries have tried to isolate it, intimidate it, sanction it into submission and bomb it into irrelevance. Now, in a remarkable inversion of regional power politics, three countries historically invested in its containment have arrived in Tehran to discuss their security with the very state they were supposed to marginalise.
The country they could not defeat is becoming the country they cannot afford to ignore.
Yesterday, Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalın met Iranian officials in an encounter whose diplomatic courtesies barely concealed its strategic significance.
The Mecca Pact, the joint defence agreement that Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan signed in Mecca in August, was supposed to consolidate a formidable Sunni-led defence alignment. Yet its representatives have come to Tehran confronting an inconvenient reality: Iran cannot be excluded from regional security merely because Washington and its partners find its independence intolerable.
Apparently, the Islamic Republic has become considerably more respectable since demonstrating that it cannot be conveniently eliminated.
This is the distinction between military destruction and strategic defeat that Washington and Israel persistently confuse. Overwhelming firepower can devastate infrastructure, assassinate officials and inflict enormous suffering. It cannot manufacture political submission.
Iran has survived military confrontation, retained retaliatory capabilities and forced neighbouring governments to reconsider the potentially catastrophic consequences of another war.
Survival becomes strategic victory when your adversaries must reorganise their calculations around it.
For Saudi Arabia, the reckoning is particularly humiliating. Riyadh spent decades treating American military supremacy as an insurance policy against Iranian influence. Yemen exposed the bankruptcy of that assumption.
Ansar Allah, Yemen’s Houthi movement, demonstrated that superior arsenals cannot guarantee security against an adversary capable of imposing disproportionate costs. The Saudi monarchy possesses spectacular weaponry, immense wealth and powerful patrons. Yet none of these has eliminated its vulnerability to Yemeni retaliation.
Now Riyadh finds itself seeking Tehran’s cooperation to manage a conflict that its military superiority has failed to resolve.
Evidently, purchasing American weapons is considerably easier than purchasing strategic security.
Pakistan’s predicament is scarcely less revealing. Munir presides over a military establishment accustomed to presenting strategic dependency as diplomatic sophistication. Islamabad’s defence commitments to Riyadh now threaten to entangle Pakistan in confrontations with Iran and Yemen that serve neither its geography nor its national interests.
The Mecca Pact promises collective security. Its less advertised feature is collective exposure to somebody else’s strategic miscalculations.
Munir must now reconcile his obligations to Saudi patrons with the inconvenient realities of Iranian power. It is an awkward assignment for an establishment that has repeatedly mistaken proximity to foreign power for genuine strategic independence.
Türkiye confronts a different calculation but reaches a similar conclusion. Ankara understands that NATO membership, military capabilities and regional ambitions cannot abolish geography. No credible security architecture can be constructed by pretending Iran is dispensable.
The deeper contradiction, however, lies within the Mecca Pact itself.
Its members seek the reassurance of collective defence while attempting to avoid being dragged into another American-Israeli confrontation. An attack on one may formally constitute an attack on all. But such commitments become considerably less attractive when Iranian retaliation, Yemeni escalation and vulnerable Gulf infrastructure enter the equation.
Collective defence sounds magnificent until someone presents the collective bill.
Iran’s achievement is not that its neighbours have embraced its revolutionary worldview. They have not. Saudi Arabia remains deeply connected to Washington, Pakistan continues its elaborate balancing act, and Türkiye remains embedded in NATO.
The significance runs deeper: these governments increasingly recognise that excluding Iran from regional security may expose them to greater dangers than engaging it.
That realisation strikes at the foundations of the American security paradigm.
For decades, Washington cultivated regional dependence on American protection while organising strategic anxieties around Iranian power. Now those same governments are exploring cooperation with the country they were encouraged to regard as an existential threat.
The irony is devastating. Decades of attempting to contain Iran may have helped establish its indispensability.
And Tehran, displaying the composure of a state conscious of its diplomatic leverage, has welcomed its visitors graciously. No triumphalist declarations are necessary. The spectacle speaks adequately for itself.
The Mecca Pact arrived ostensibly to discuss regional stability. What it encountered was the strategic consequence of its own failed assumptions.
Iran did not have to join the alliance. The alliance had to come to Iran.
