articles.title: Russian court jails IT company director for 13 years over crypto donations after Binance shared his data, rights group says
articles.body:
A Russian court sentenced Yuri Belenky, director of the IT company DiHouse, to 13 years in prison on terrorism financing charges, Radio Liberty reported on 26 October. The case concerns cryptocurrency donations that investigators believe were meant for Ukraine’s Armed Forces, the outlet said. The court also fined Belenky 500,000 rubles ($6,200), according to the report.
Since 2022, Russian courts have imprisoned Russians and Ukrainians under treason, terrorism, and other national-security laws over donations to Ukrainian causes. Binance, one of the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchanges, left Russia in 2023 but says it cooperates with lawful law-enforcement requests in different countries.
Belenky had lived in Bulgaria with his wife and child since 2015. In September 2025, he traveled to Moscow on business, and police detained him at the airport for allegedly using obscene language, Radio Liberty reported. In court, Belenky denied swearing, but the judge gave him 13 days of administrative detention. On the 10th day of his detention, Russia’s Investigative Committee opened a criminal case against him under an article on terrorism financing, based on a report from the Federal Security Service, according to the report.
Binance shared account records with Russian investigators, rights group says
In October 2025, Russia’s Investigative Committee contacted Binance to request information on six users who had transferred funds to a cryptocurrency wallet published by journalist Arkady Babchenko, the Russian human rights project First Department said on 17 August 2026. The exchange provided investigators with Belenky’s detailed account history, including his personal information, copies of identification documents, and cryptocurrency transaction records, according to the organization. The human rights project said the materials helped investigators identify nine more transfers, which went into the final charge against Belenky. Binance told his lawyer it does not give law enforcement user account data without a court order or an equivalent ruling, the group said.
Belenky’s alleged offense was transferring donations totaling 126,000 rubles ($1,560) between 2022 and 2024 to an account published by Babchenko, Radio Liberty reported. The court ordered that sum confiscated.
Russia sentences Ukrainian women from Zaporizhzhia Oblast to 14 years for donating $120 to Ukrainian forces
The court said the money in Babchenko’s account went to Ukraine’s Armed Forces and the Azov battalion, which Russia designates as a terrorist organization, Radio Liberty reported.
In a statement dated 14 October 2025, Babchenko said he had not received transfers from Belenky to the cryptocurrency wallets he had published. He emphasized that he had raised money for civilian humanitarian needs, not to support the military.
Binance’s exit from Russia and previous data-sharing concerns
In September 2023, Binance announced that it would sell its entire Russian business to cryptocurrency exchange CommEX, according to the company’s website. Operating in Russia was incompatible with Binance’s compliance strategy, the exchange’s chief compliance officer, Noah Perlman, said in the announcement. Binance said it would fully exit the Russian market, receive no share of future revenue from the sale, and retain no option to buy back the business.
CommEX said on 29 September 2023 that it was not owned by Binance but confirmed that it had hired some former Binance employees during the platform’s six-month development, Cointelegraph reported.
UK sanctions crypto exchanges and “A7 network” in crackdown on Russian evasion systems
The exit came after earlier questions about Binance’s dealings with the Russian state. In April 2021, Russian financial intelligence officials met with Binance’s head of Eastern Europe and Russia in Moscow and asked the exchange to provide customer data, including names and addresses, Reuters reported in April 2022. The Binance executive agreed to the request in a message to a business associate, saying he didn’t have “much of a choice,” the outlet said. Binance told Reuters it had never been contacted by Russian authorities about Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny.
In February 2026, 11 US senators asked the Treasury Department and the Justice Department to investigate Binance’s compliance with sanctions and anti-money laundering rules, Cointelegraph reported. They cited reports that about $1.7 billion had moved through Binance to Iran-linked entities, as well as possible activity related to evading Russian sanctions. The senators also warned that Binance payment cards launched in parts of the former Soviet Union could facilitate sanctions evasion. Binance rejected the allegations.

articles.title: Satellite images confirm damage at Russia’s largest known air defense storage base after Ukrainian drone strike
articles.body:
Satellite images show signs of fires at the 75th Arsenal facility in Serpukhov in the Moscow Region, around 60 miles south of the Russian capital, Greenpeace analysts who examined the imagery told The Insider. The site was struck by Ukrainian drones overnight into Oct. 22. The target was the largest known Russian storage base for air defense equipment.
Satellite images from Oct. 26 show changes compared with earlier imagery. Greenpeace experts who analyzed the data told The Insider that burn marks are visible in the upper left of the image. Additional signs of fire can be seen in the center near a hangar and in the lower left.
The Ukrainian open source intelligence (OSINT) project Oko Hora ✙ News and Analytics claims that the strikes hit workshops No. 24 and No. 25, which specialize in repairing and restoring components for Russia’s S-300V and Buk surface-to-air missile systems, its Tunguska-M air defense systems, and radar equipment. The site, formerly an arsenal of the Russian Defense Ministry’s Main Missile and Artillery Directorate (GRAU), only became the largest known storage base for air defense equipment in Russia after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
OSINT analyst Jompy wrote in March 2024 that researchers had identified an air defense equipment storage base at the 75th Arsenal site in Serpukhov, adding that the facility had originally served as an artillery depot before being repurposed to store air defense systems. Satellite images show numerous hangars at the site that may contain systems including the Buk or S-300. The analyst said it appeared to be the largest known storage base for air defense and surface-to-air missile systems in Russia.
Another OSINT analyst, Athene Noctua, wrote in June 2024 that the 75th Arsenal base held about 60% of the identified reserve of Russian Ground Forces air defense equipment — 574 out of 950 units.

articles.title: Turkey committee approves pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkish parliamentary committee approves defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan
A Turkish parliamentary committee approved a defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan on Tuesday, as tensions between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi rebels grow.
The defence agreement commits the sides to regard an armed attack against one as an attack on all three. The foreign affairs committee approved it with votes from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's ruling party and its allies, despite objections from the opposition.
The agreement now goes to the full assembly for a debate and a vote. No date has been set.
The 16-article Mecca Joint Defence Agreement also paves the way for military cooperation, joint weapons production, technology transfers and intelligence sharing. The pact binds the parties for 10 years, according to the agreement published by Turkish state media.
Ministers from the grouping have already met twice, in Istanbul and Riyadh, while high-level delegations from the three countries held talks in Tehran on Monday to try to avert renewed fighting in the Iran war.
Turkish government officials say they are considering sending military support to Saudi Arabia, but that the agreement is defensive and that no Turkish troops will be deployed to fight in Yemen or to attack the Houthis.
Ruling Justice and Development Party legislator Fuat Oktay, who heads the committee, urged fellow members to approve the pact, arguing that it aims to increase deterrence and cooperation, does not target other countries and is likely to contribute to peace and stability.
"The agreements our country has signed and to which it is a party are not intended for aggression, expansionism, or the formation of a bloc against third countries," Oktay said.
"On the contrary, our nation is a party to defence agreements aimed at strengthening deterrence, fortifying our region and fostering peace and stability."
Opposition parties warned the agreement could put Turkish soldiers in harm's way and embroil the country in other nations' conflicts.
"Will this agreement enhance the security of the peoples involved, or will it create new obligations that entangle Turkey in the wars of other nations?" asked Semra Caglar Gokalp of the pro-Kurdish Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party.
Pointing to conflicts between Pakistan and India and tensions along Pakistan's border with Afghanistan, she continued: "What are the limits of the responsibility Turkey might assume in the face of these challenges?"
The opposition has also criticised the parties for holding meetings before parliament has ratified the pact.

articles.title: Putin turns a half-hour call with European leaders into a 90-minute history lecture. Trump says a three-way summit could happen ‘very soon.’
articles.body:
Putin turns a half-hour call with European leaders into a 90-minute history lecture. Trump says a three-way summit could happen ‘very soon.’
Trump hopes a trilateral meeting with Putin and Volodymyr Zelensky will happen soon. The U.S. president told reporters such a meeting could take place “very soon” and said he expects the summit to achieve “a lot of progress.” He did not say where or when the talks might occur.
Plans for a trilateral meeting of U.S., Ukrainian, and Russian delegations have become clearer. Ukrainian President Zelensky said that after a call between Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre with Vladimir Putin, “there is a sense that the Russians are serious about meeting in Abu Dhabi.”
Zelensky said the talks in Abu Dhabi are expected to address “de-escalation steps in the energy sector and at sea, as well as the exchange and return home of prisoners.” He added that there is also hope “to discuss the format in which a trilateral meeting at the leaders’ level could take place.”
During the call, Putin lectured the Finnish president and the Norwegian prime minister on the history of the Slavs. As a result, the call stretched to nearly an hour and a half instead of the planned half hour, Financial Times sources said. The Kremlin’s press service, commenting on the call, said “Putin assessed the current situation in the conflict zone in Ukraine, recalling its root causes.” The FT reported that an immediate ceasefire was not discussed during the call.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticized Stubb and Støre for the call with Putin. She said the initiative had not been coordinated with the rest of the EU countries. The Finnish president responded by saying that he and Støre “held the conversation in our capacity as leaders of our respective countries, not as representatives of Europe.” The European Union is trying to choose who will represent it in talks with Russia. Stubb has been named as one of the most likely candidates, with his good relationship with Donald Trump cited as one of the factors.
EU representatives also plan to take part in the talks in Abu Dhabi. According to Euronews, the delegation will be led by Björn Seibert, head of the Cabinet of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. A meeting in this format — with representatives from the U.S., Ukraine, Russia, and the European Union — would be the first since the start of the full-scale war, the broadcaster said.
The war in photographs
Russian forces struck Kharkiv overnight on October 28, and a drone attack set an apartment building on fire in the city’s Osnovianskyi district. The attack killed a 60-year-old man and injured four people, said Oleh Syniehubov, head of the regional military administration. It also set fire to a private home, an industrial building, and several outbuildings.

articles.title: French Frigate Intercepts Ballistic Missile in Red Sea
articles.body:
A French Navy frigate intercepted a ballistic missile near the Belgian minehunter Primula while escorting the vessel in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait area.
Baird Maritime reported the incident, citing confirmation from the French Armed Forces General Staff on October 27.
According to the French military command, the incident occurred on October 13, 2026, while the French frigate was escorting a Belgian Tripartite-class minehunter.
The French General Staff emphasized that the crew’s actions were purely defensive. No one was injured, and neither vessel sustained damage.
Belgian newspaper De Morgen first reported the interception on October 26. Belgium’s Ministry of Defense subsequently confirmed the information to VRT NWS journalists.
Initial assessments suggest that the missile may have been launched by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, who have attacked vessels in the Red Sea. However, their involvement has not been officially confirmed.
The French military command has not disclosed the name of the frigate that carried out the interception or the type of surface-to-air missile used.
A French Ministry of the Armed Forces operational update for October 8-15 reported that a FREMM-class multipurpose frigate was operating in the Red Sea, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Gulf of Aden as part of the European Union’s EUNAVFOR ASPIDES operation.
One of the French ships operating in the area was the frigate Languedoc. In early October, it shot down a drone while escorting the CMA CGM Champs Elysées container ship through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
However, no confirmation currently indicates that Languedoc intercepted the ballistic missile on October 13.
The Belgian Primula (M924) belongs to the Tripartite class of mine countermeasures vessels, jointly developed by Belgium, the Netherlands, and France.
The ship is designed to search for, identify, and neutralize naval mines. However, it lacks the missile-defense systems needed to independently counter ballistic threats.
According to Belgium’s Ministry of Defense, on May 28, Primula and the Dutch minehunter Willemstad departed Zeebrugge for the Mediterranean to join NATO’s Standing NATO Mine Countermeasures Group 2 (SNMCMG2).
The deployment was also intended to enable the Belgian vessel to participate in potential mine-clearing operations in the Strait of Hormuz, should the relevant political decision be made.

articles.title: European leaders are ‘political masochists’ – Lavrov
articles.body:
European leaders are ‘political masochists’ – Lavrov
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has branded European leaders “political masochists,” accusing them of sacrificing their own citizens’ welfare in pursuit of Russia’s defeat in Ukraine.
Speaking to editors-in-chief of African media outlets in Moscow on Tuesday, Lavrov accused Western governments of pressuring their populations to accept declining living standards to secure Ukraine’s victory in conflict with Russia. 
“They are trying to keep public opinion in a position where people must sacrifice everything: salaries, jobs, healthcare services and social benefits in general, so that Ukraine defeats Russia,” Lavrov said. “People can feel how their situation is deteriorating in European countries,” he added.
He singled out German Chancellor Friedrich Merz as one of the politicians advocating such an approach. “These are masochists, political masochists, if you like,” the foreign minister said.
Merz has defended Germany’s growing military spending and continued support for Kiev while warning that the country can no longer afford its existing welfare system.
The German government has tightened welfare rules, introducing benefit reductions of 30% for repeated violations and, in some cases, complete withdrawal. Berlin’s proposed 2027 budget also envisages billions of euros in savings from pensions, healthcare and other social programs.
Germany has meanwhile earmarked €11.6 billion for Ukraine in 2027, alongside plans to raise defense spending to record levels.
Britain, another major backer of Kiev, has also reduced welfare payments, nearly halving health-related benefits for most new claimants under Universal Credit, a program supporting low-income households and people unable to work.
In September, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called for further welfare cuts to fund increased military spending. “We need to fund our defence, not spend all our money on welfare,” she said. The government, however, rejected her proposal.
France has likewise pursued spending restraint, including a proposed public-sector pay freeze, while increasing military expenditure. The measures have faced opposition from trade unions protesting declining purchasing power and deteriorating public services.
Public discontent has fueled widespread protests across Europe in recent weeks, with hundreds of thousands demonstrating in France over rising living costs, education funding and inequality. Tens of thousands have also taken to the streets in Spain and Portugal over soaring housing costs, while Italy has seen protests over declining living standards.
European NATO members have committed to substantially increasing defense expenditure, citing the perceived threat from Russia.
Russian President Vladimir Putin last week rejected repeated claims that Moscow was preparing for war with Europe, describing them as part of an ongoing “anti-Russian campaign” on the continent. “They now go so far as to constantly speak of a ‘Russian threat’ and even discuss preparations for a war with Russia – which, in my view, amounts to a kind of political schizophrenia. But I hope that it will pass,” Putin stated.
Moscow has repeatedly dismissed claims that it intends to attack NATO countries as “nonsense,” accusing Western leaders of using the alleged Russian threat to justify militarization and continued support for Kiev.

articles.title: Gulf states working on multipart peace deal to avert renewal of US-Iran war
articles.body:
A multipronged peace deal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within four days of sanctions being lifted and for the Houthis to withdraw substantial forces inside Yemen are at the heart of Gulf states’ plans to avert what they regard as a disastrous renewal of war between Iran and the US.
The US is aware of the talks’ progress but is holding out for a concession that European powers suggest could involve Iran allowing UN weapons inspectors back into the country.
The British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, urged the Iranians to agree to readmit the UN weapons inspectors when he met the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, in New York but so far Iran has refused, saying it will only hold talks in principle on its nuclear programme.
European diplomats believe allowing weapons inspectors to reenter Iran and visit its bombed nuclear sites is a minimum requirement for a breakthrough with the US president, Donald Trump.
But Iran remains focused solely on the guarantees of sanctions relief it would receive in return for reopening the strait of Hormuz. Dr Ali Bagheri, the deputy secretary of Iran’s national security council, said Iran was willing to reduce its proposal that the strait reopen seven days after economic sanctions are lifted to four days.
In a further sign of flexibility, Iran is starting to acknowledge it has a mediating role in the parallel conflict in Yemen. Iran’s secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, met the Houthi’s ambassador to Iran, Ibrahim al-Dulaimi, on Tuesday.
The meeting took place 24 hours after a high-level delegation from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan travelled to Tehran to discuss Saudi terms for ending the Yemen conflict as well as a longer-term security architecture for the region.
Iran backs the Houthis, and has the power to influence them, including devising proposals that stop short of a Houthi military victory that many say is unobtainable. In return the Houthis are demanding that Saudi Arabia lift what it regards as a naval and air blockade on Houthi-held territory.
Iran successfully prevented discussion of its nuclear programme at the meeting with Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, and instead ensured the focus was a broader discussion about a long-term regional security vision that would include the Gulf states and Iran and see the US presence in the Middle East reduced or ended.
A new non-aggression pact in which Iran is no longer ostracised by the rest of the Gulf, as it has been since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, would meet Iran’s highest strategic goal.
An agreed commitment to this goal by six Gulf states might also make it easier for Iran to swallow potentially difficult tactical concessions that it would be required to make concerning its nuclear programme.
One of the key advocates of the inclusive security plan, Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, said he believed the US administration understood this was the direction the region is heading.
He said: “I think if Iran is fully re-engaged in this idea of having all of us, eight countries at peace with the rest of the world, the economic potential is going to be enormous for all of us in the region and those outside the region who choose to take part in this development. We have really discussed this in at length during the talks between Iran and the United States, and I think there is general acceptance that this will be the direction of travel once we have a deal in place at the end of the day.”
At a televised event in Iran this week Araghchi underlined the importance of a new postwar security pact to Iran, saying: “Recently, there has been talk of a new war but I am already thinking about the postwar period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same.”

articles.title: Qatari mediators present Iran with new deal to end the war, official says
articles.body:
By Andrew Mills and Parisa Hafezi
Oct 28 (Reuters) - Qatari mediators have presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war with the US and Israel, an official briefed on the negotiations said, but a senior Iranian official said Doha had only put forward unacceptable ideas that did not amount to an offer.
The official briefed on the negotiations, who is not from Iran, said a new draft peace proposal for the eight-month-old conflict was presented on Sunday and was being considered by Tehran, with a response expected by the end of the week.
Qatar, along with Pakistan, has led mediation to end the war, which has disrupted global shipping and oil supplies and recently spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
The proposal presented by Qatar sets a seven-day timeline addressing both Tehran’s and Washington’s concerns, laying out daily confidence-building steps that each side must take, the official briefed on the negotiations said. The timeline could begin early next week and several countries would act as guarantors of the deal, the official added.
Shortly afterwards, a senior Iranian official involved in the talks said Qatar had presented only “unacceptable ideas and not an offer”, and that Tehran’s policy on showing no flexibility over the nuclear issue remained unchanged.
Washington wants Iran’s decades-long nuclear programme to be part of negotiations to end the war from the outset, while Iran says its conditions — which include an end to the US blockade of Iranian ports and the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports — must be met first. Iran rejects Western concerns that its nuclear programme is military in nature.
ATTACK ON SAUDI OIL REFINERY
In late September, Iran presented another seven-day proposal under which Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy shipping channels, could be reopened if certain conditions were met. US President Donald Trump rejected it, prompting further Qatari mediation.
The draft discussed in Tehran on Sunday was different from that proposal, the official briefed on the negotiations said, though the details of the latest plan were not immediately clear. The official had previously told Reuters that the Qatari mediators had coordinated with Washington before going to Tehran.
Earlier mediation efforts to end the war that the US and Israel launched on February 28 helped produce an interim peace agreement in June, but it quickly unravelled.
In recent weeks, Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi forces have launched repeated attacks against Saudi Arabia — a key US ally and the world’s largest crude exporter — opening a new front in the eight-month-old war.
Oil prices rose more than 1% to more than $115 per barrel on Wednesday after a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s largest oil refinery, Ras Tanura, stoking concerns over supply risks.
Fighting with the Houthis intensified last month as the militant group advanced against Saudi-backed forces towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another important shipping lane on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula from Hormuz.
CONCERNS ABOUT RISK OF NEW STRIKES
The official briefed on the negotiations said there were concerns ahead of Sunday’s meeting in Tehran that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, fighting for another term in a general election, could resume attacks on the Islamic Republic this week.
On Friday, US President Donald Trump repeated threats to strike Iran again, while Iranian security officials told Reuters Tehran had drawn up detailed plans to attack Gulf undersea cables if the US and Israel resumed attacks.
On Monday, top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan also met Iranian officials in Tehran as part of de-escalation efforts. Qatar said on Tuesday that Iran needs to stop threats against Arab Gulf states and open the Strait of Hormuz to show good intentions for mediation efforts to succeed.
Gulf states came under sustained bombardment earlier in the war.
The war also reignited fighting between Israel and the Iran-backed Lebanese armed group Hezbollah. It has eroded Trump’s approval ratings ahead of the US midterm elections that decide control of Congress.
(Reporting by Andrew Mills and Parisa Hafezi; Writing by Nayera Adballah; Editing by Aidan Lewis)

articles.title: Defense Intelligence of Ukraine Exposes Network of Companies Developing Russia’s Rassvet Satellite Communications System
articles.body:
The Defense Intelligence of Ukraine has identified 49 Russian and Belarusian companies involved in developing Russia’s Rassvet low-Earth-orbit satellite communications system.
The War&Sanctions portal reported on this.
According to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, the project involves IT companies, microelectronics manufacturers, research institutes, enterprises of the Russian State Corporation for Space Activities “Roscosmos,” and organizations linked to Russia’s Ministry of Defense.
Of the 49 companies and institutions identified, 23, including Roscosmos, are not under sanctions imposed by any country in the international sanctions coalition.
The following companies and organizations are involved in the project:
Once the satellite constellation is fully deployed, it is intended to provide strategic communications, support command and control of troops and strike platforms, transmit data from unmanned systems, and equip command posts and military vehicles with satellite terminals.
According to information published by Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, these plans will be implemented once the orbital constellation reaches 292 satellites.
The system’s priority coverage area will include Ukraine and EU countries. Intelligence officials warn that, once it achieves sufficient coverage, Russia could also use the system to conduct hybrid operations against other countries.
The Rassvet system consists of a low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation, ground-based control infrastructure, gateway stations, and subscriber terminals for fixed and mobile platforms.
In July, Russian satellites provided at least two communication windows per day over Ukraine, each lasting more than an hour.
In October, the first satellite from the second batch reached an operational altitude of around 500 km. That same month, Bureau 1440 unveiled three types of user terminals designed to connect to the satellite system.
The article “Electronic Warfare Against Rassvet: Why Ukraine Needs to Act Now” analysed the capabilities of EW means to counter Russia’s satellite communications system.
